title: The Sun Was In My Eyes And Other Sorry Excuses Are Being Polished And Perfected Via Use Of Generative AI
text:
Excuses, excuses, excuses.
Seems like everyone these days has an endless supply of excuses. Even the latest twists and turns in the political realm have been rampant with excuses touting and explaining high-profile debate woes such as being too tired, having had a cold, suffering from jet lag, being distracted by others, and a slew of other stated or implied “my dog ate my homework” excusable conditions.
Excuses are what make the world go round.
Thus, knowing about excuses and their ins and outs is an extremely valuable skill. Your excuse-making can always benefit from additional honing. Think of things this way. Is your current capacity of excuse-making the best that it can be? Is there more that you could do to improve your excuse-making prowess? I dare say the answer is a likely yes.
To fully answer these probing questions, we need to look closely at the nature of excuses, including the rather innovative perspective that modern-day generative AI can be your best pal when devising, polishing, and perfecting your humankind excuses.
Yes, believe it or not, another handy-dandy use of generative AI and large language models (LLMs) consists of leaning into them as your online always-on excuse-making factory. You can do this easily in just about any major generative AI app, such as ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, Bard, and others. Furthermore, and I’m sure this is a big relief, you can access a generative AI app on a 24/7 basis, thus, no matter what day it is or what time it is, the ability to readily generate a whopper of an excuse is right there at your fingertips.
I refer to this not as excuse-making but as AI-powered excuse-generation.
You are aiming to use generative AI to generate excuses for you. Ergo, it is sensibly referred to as excuse-generation. Our AI friend in need, when the need presents itself, indeed. Thank you, generative AI.
Let’s unpack the whole kit and kaboodle on this.
Before we leap into the details, allow me to go into my customary opening remarks.
For my ongoing readers, in today’s column, I am continuing my in-depth series about the impact of generative AI in the health and medical realm. The focus this time is once again on the mental health domain and examines the use of generative AI in support of humankind's excuse-making. There are decidedly mental health ramifications associated with the excuses we come up with, how we use them, when we use them, and other related behavioral and cognitive considerations.
I have previously examined numerous interleaving facets of generative AI and mental health, see my comprehensive overview at the link here. You might also find of notable interest a CBS 60 Minutes episode that recently examined crucial facets of this evolving topic, see the link here (I am honored and pleased to indicate that I was featured in the episode, see the link here).
Other vital background includes my in-depth coverage of mental health chatbots which have been bolstered by generative AI (see the link here) and the rapidly changing nature of the client-therapist relationship due to generative AI at the link here. I explored where things are headed regarding the levels of AI-based mental therapy autonomous guidance at the link here, and showcased the importance of the World Health Organization (WHO) report on global health and generative AI at the link here, and so on.
Vital Ins And Outs About Excuses
There is a lot that can be said in favor of and in opposition to excuses.
It might be proclaimed that excuses grease the skids of life. Someone forgets a friend’s birthday and proffers an excuse for why they failed to timely provide birthday wishes. The receiver of the excuse might think that the birthday greeting oversight itself was relatively modest and thus readily accept the excuse. The world is right and good once again.
On the other hand, the person might be utterly steamed that their birthday had been overlooked. No excuse will do. Well, if the excuse was momentous, perhaps it might indeed suffice, such as a circumstance where the person had been kidnapped by space aliens and was beamed up into the night sky into a spaceship and was unable to grant birthday wishes while ensnared. That’s an impressive excuse.
Excuses though must usually be proportionate and reasonable to be considered proper and acceptable. Did the person truly get beamed up by alien beings? This raises the eyebrows and makes the excuse quite suspect. Too much blarney is unlikely to get you out of the doghouse. Sometimes, admittedly, excessive blarney can turn things into a humor-laden affair and perhaps the receiver laughs so hard that they accept the excuse and move on to other matters.
Twists and turns are the bread and butter of excuses and using excuses.
If you don’t offer an excuse, the receiver might get upset at your failing to provide one. Oddly enough, they might not especially care what the excuse is. The concern is that a lack of an excuse suggests that you don’t respect them enough to provide one. Ergo, society generally expects the giving of an excuse.
If you do offer an excuse and it is a lame excuse, the receiver might not like that either. You are darned when you don’t provide an excuse. You are also darned if you provide a lousy or lame excuse. By and large, excuses are to be of the revered Goldilocks variety, balancing between being too cold and too hot as the porridge goes.
Difficulties abound. If you provide a good excuse, but the person didn’t want an excuse and didn’t expect one, you have likely shot your own foot. Sad face. Suppose that a person expected an excuse, you provided one that you thought was good, but they thought it was a lame excuse. Viewpoints on whether an excuse is either good or lame can vary dramatically. One person’s good excuse is another person’s bad excuse.
Baffling at times.
Let’s keep going. You opt to come up with an excuse. Turns out that it takes precious time to figure out your excuse. Toil and sweat ensue. Finally, you have an excuse that will knock the socks off the receiver. You deliver the excuse. The receiver yawns, politely says thanks, and acts as though the excuse is hardly worth telling. Anger swells within you. By gosh, you put a lot of hard labor into that excuse, and it isn’t getting the proper due that it deserves.
This is where many people make a fatal error. They try to impress the receiver that the excuse ought to bring them to tears. This was an Oscar-winning excuse. They did not appreciate the effort that went into it. Oops, the person now starts to dig into the excuse. Your initial hope was that the receiver would blindly accept the excuse, but now, by your own doing, they are giving you the proverbial third degree.
Mistakes can happen when it comes to excuses.
Quite a lot of the time.
Tip Of The Iceberg About Excuses
Must an excuse be the truth?
Aha, that gets a tremendous amount of debate going. Some would insist that an excuse must always be the truth. If you say that your dog ate your homework then by gosh, the dog must have done so, or else you are fibbing. An excuse based on a lie is a house of cards. The receiver of the excuse can potentially bring the house of cards crashing down by interrogating you about the excuse.
A fully true excuse is presumably unable to be shaken. A receiver might question whether the excuse merits your transgression, but fortunately, they won’t catch you in a lie. Your head is held high that you honorably told the truth. It could be that the excuse is flimsy, and you ought to not have allowed the excuse to stop you from whatever you were obligated to do. You will get dinged for that. The truth though is the honest truth, honestly so.
There are shady excuses that border the truth and a lie. Consider this. Maybe your dog ate your homework because you purposely handed the homework to your dog. Wink-wink, your dog at your homework. You conveniently and necessarily omitted the part where you instigated the excuse. This is somewhere in the vicinity of a lie (some would say it absolutely is a lie).
Lies often permeate excuses. The entire excuse might be a lie, or maybe just elements here or there. It is said that if you are going to embed any lies, the excuse can potentially withstand scrutiny by infusing truths too, seeking to hide, disguise, or mask any lies. If there is no truth included, the lies are going to be readily vulnerable to attack. By having embedded truths, you can use the ploy of sticking with those truth portions and pretend to be outraged that the excuse is being challenged. Meanwhile, you desperately avoid venturing into the lie portions to hopefully distract the receiver accordingly.
I’d like to somewhat formalize the excuses realm by noting these four key factors:
- (1) Excuse-making. This is the process of coming up with an excuse. Some do so carefully, others do so off the top of their head. Circumstances vary. People vary.
- (2) Excuse-giver. This is the person that is going to deliver the excuse. They might have undertaken the excuse-making by themselves, or they could have sought others for assistance in doing so.
- (3) Excuse-receiver. This is the person that is going to receive the excuse. They might accept the excuse, they might challenge the excuse, and otherwise, all manner of responses and reactions can arise.
- (4) Excuse-generation. This is a new term that I’ve coined to describe the act of leaning into generative AI to aid in the excuse-making process. I’ll be telling you more about this momentarily. Hang in there, it is a doozy.
Lots and lots of rules about excuses exist, such as but not limited to:
- Excuses can be based on pure truth, or can be composed of some lies, or entirely consist of a lie.
- Excuses might be short and sweet, or can be modestly involved, or can be intricate and lengthy.
- Excuses at times are only offered when requested, other times are offered due to unspoken expectations, or other considerations.
- Excuse-making can rely upon common excuses that are used all the time.
- Excuse-making can produce seemingly novelties, unique or attention-getting excuses.
- The excuse can be more important than the transgression and overpower the underlying faux pas.
- The excuse can be unimportant and merely a mindless checkmark that an excuse was provided.
- Etc.
We begin to learn about excuses at the earliest ages of our existence.
A child right away discovers that excuses can be a crucial tool in life. They witness others using excuses and perceive what works and what doesn’t work. How their parents react to excuses is an important shaping condition. Kids will make use of excuses and refine their methodology as they grow. Often, you can trace adult uses of excuses to what transpired in their childhood and learn often by the seat of their pants about the nature of excuses.
There aren’t classes you take in school that particularly teach you about excuses. Most of the time, you garner the range and impact of excuses by trial and error. No one gives you a textbook and says that here is everything you need to know about excuses. And the only testing associated with excuses is how they work out in real life.
We don’t usually talk about excuse-making in explicit ways.
There is a tendency to pretend that excuses aren’t as prevalent as they are. One problem is that this means that people are left to their own whimsy trying to figure out how to cope with and undertake excuse-making. You likely encounter people who are very good at it and encounter other people who flounder at it.
That’s what happens when no formalized training or direct instruction occurs in the realm of excuses. Of course, any effort to make excuse-making into a real thing would instantly get crushed by the pronouncement that excuses are bad stuff. An angry exhortation will right away ask incredulously, how in the world can you go out of your way to teach someone about the use of excuses? You might as well teach them how to cheat and steal.
There you have it, excuses run the world, but we keep our heads in the sand about the importance of excuses and excuse-making.
Life is tough that way.
Mental Health And Excuses Are A Thing
Mental health aspects enter the picture when you macroscopically look at excuses.
Suppose a person is always using excuses. They are riddled with excuses. We often will ask whether the person seems mentally fit since they seem to overly rely on excuses. Daily existence allows for a semblance of excuses, but excessive reliance raises mental health concerns.
An intriguing bent of the excessive use of excuses is when someone provides excuses principally based on their self-claim that they have mental health issues. This is how that goes. A person provides an excuse, and let’s say the excuse is summarily rejected by the receiver. What now? The person giving the excuse might apologize and explain that they have a mental health condition that implores them to make excuses. In a sense, this is yet another excuse (which might be true or might be false). They are relying on a claim of a mental health concern as a gambit for a form of excuse.
On a related tangent, you might find of interest my extensive look at the somewhat surprising revelation that people often lie to their therapists, see the link here. In theory, people ought to be truthful to their therapist. Patients or clients are presumably undermining their therapy by employing half-truths or lies. Well, surprise upon surprise, excuses are also at times part and parcel of those seeking and undertaking mental health therapy.
Allow me to explain.
While getting mental health guidance, people are at times tempted to lie. Some lies are perhaps small, such as an excuse that is a lie about why they showed up late to the therapy session. I got stuck in traffic might be a lie that is given as an excuse, when the real story is that the person had forgotten where they had put their keys and, in a total panic, turned their home upside down to find the keys. Is that a small lie or a big one, ergo, is it a small excuse or a big excuse?
The therapist might be working with the client or patient on matters pertinent to this type of forgetfulness and panic, but the excuse or lie about getting stuck in traffic seeks to hide that otherwise relevant behavior. The excuse unfortunately is going to undercut the therapy. I mention this to highlight that many of the lies told during therapy are also cooked into excuses. Well-trained professional therapists are watchful of those weighty matters.
Here's another angle on excuses and mental health.
A person realizes they have become dependent upon excuses and excuse-making. It has started to dominate their work and home life. For this alone, the person might seek out mental health advice. They want to know how they can curtail their propensity to use excuses. Why are they always relying on excuses? Does it mean something?
To clarify, I’m not saying that all matters involving excuses are somehow a mental health issue. That is an imprudent proposition. As earlier noted, excuses make the world go round. This doesn’t imply that there are always mental health conditions at stake, nor does it imply that there are never any mental health facets involved.
Research About Excuses And Excuse-Making
Let’s look at some research related to excuses and excuse-making.
You might be astounded at how many excuses we invoke over a typical year. In an article entitled “This Is How Many Excuses The Average American Makes Every Day” by Zoya Gervis, New York Post, May 18, 2020, these eye-opening stats are mentioned (excerpts):
- “The average American will make 2,190 excuses to validate their decisions per year, according to new research.”
- “A poll of 2,000 Americans found that the average respondent makes six excuses daily, adding up to over 2K excuses each year.”
- “And results revealed the ever-popular “I’m too tired” topped the list of common excuses (49 percent). That was followed by the commonly given excuse of “I don’t have enough money” (48 percent), with “I don’t have enough time” (48 percent) rounding out the top three.”
- “On a weekly basis, excuses were most commonly given by respondents in order to avoid exercising, eating healthy and running errands — all tied at 33 percent. Beyond that, 29 percent admit to employing excuses to get out of social events each week and 28 percent make weekly excuses for not wearing sunscreen.”
Are you keeping up with your fellow Americans by ensuring that you use at least six excuses per day?
I trust so.
The basis for why we use excuses has a multitude of sensible reasons. It can be a sense of control, and there is also a likely element of wanting to reduce guilt. In an article entitled “Excuses: Why Do We Rationalize Our Wrongdoings?” by Mary Lamla, Psychology Today, November 29, 2019, these salient points were made (excerpts):
- “Since we are capable of experiencing shame and guilt, we want to lessen the perceived and potential blame from others or any self-blame we attach to an offense or fault.”
- “The perceived benefit associated with an excuse also includes having a sense of control over one’s life and attempts to view the wrongdoing as an anomaly. In such cases, behavior that is paired with an excuse shifts the responsibility for the cause of an event to an external force, which is considered to be more effective than no explanation or an apology alone.”
- “However, if you have a history of failing to meet an expected standard, others may respond negatively to behavior that is reoccurring, regardless of any apology or excuse.”
- “Excuses may be perceived as seeking forgiveness and mitigating personal responsibility, which might lessen the anger of the wronged party. However, excuse-making may also be considered to be a conscious attempt to manipulate the emotions of others—a naïve theory of emotion that links managing the emotions of others in ways that lead to positive outcomes.”
What is the reason or set of reasons that you harbor when you use excuses? One supposes that the reasons can be context-dependent.
The act of excuse-making is both art and science. In a now-classic article from 1988 entitled “Excuses: Their Effective Role In The Negotiation Of Reality” by C. Synder and Raymond Higgins, Psychological Bulletin, 1988, these keystones were indicated (excerpts):
- “Excuse-making is defined here as the process of shifting causal attributions for negative personal outcomes from sources that are relatively more central to the person's sense of self to sources that are relatively less central, thereby resulting in perceived benefits to the person's image and sense of control.”
- “This definition is used to examine the image- and control-related effects of excuse-making on the variables of emotional states (self-esteem, anxiety, depression), health, and performance. “
- “Generally, excuse-making appears to have positive benefits for the excuse-giver.”
- “The sequence of events whereby excuses work to maintain the individual's image and sense of control at the personal and interpersonal levels is also analyzed. “
If you are keenly interested in the underlying precepts of excuses, the above-noted article is considered by many as a crucial research study. That being said, I’d like to note that excuse-making can have positive benefits for the excuse-giver but can also have negative costs. It is vital to see both sides of the coin.
Let’s cover two more research-oriented studies and we will move on and cover the role of generative AI in the excuses realm.
A research study entitled “Excuses and Character: Personal and Social Implications of Excuses” by Barry Schlenker, Beth Pontari, and Andrew Christopher, Personality And Social Psychology Review, February 2001, made these points (excerpts):
- “Excuses are self-serving explanations or accounts, that aim to reduce personal responsibility for questionable events, thereby disengaging core components of the self from the incident.”
- “Their goal is to convince audiences, often the actor included, that a questionable event is not as much the actor's fault as it might otherwise appear to be; and to the extent that the actor is at fault, the incident is portrayed as springing from less central rather than more central aspects of self (e.g., carelessness rather than stupidity).”
- “The disadvantages of excuses have been relatively neglected.”
- “On the disadvantage side, excuse-makers risk being seen as deceptive, self-absorbed, and ineffectual; they are viewed as unreliable social participants with flawed characters. These undesired consequences result when excuses are used in ways that lower credibility (e.g., fail to receive corroboration), lower goodwill (e.g., blame failures on team members), and produce long-term disengagement (e.g., lead to failures to correct personal deficiencies).”
I brought up that article due to the emphasis included on the downsides of excuses.
Finally, in a relatively recent article entitled “Using Mental Health As An Excuse For Bad Behavior” by Nicholas Balaisis, Psychology Today, January 5, 2023, here were some notable aspects (excerpts):
- “As awareness of mental health issues has grown, so too has the prevalence of people blaming their bad behavior on ‘poor mental health.’"
- “This may appear in sentences like: “I can’t go to work because it is bad for my mental health,” “I can’t talk about this issue because it negatively affects my mental health,” or most dangerous of all, “I was a jerk because I am suffering from mental health issues that are beyond my control.”
- “Using one's mental health as a standalone reason for negative behaviors can sometimes be a form of psychological avoidance.”
- “Taking responsibility for your mental health means looking beyond immediate distressing situations to broader psychological origins and roots.”
- “In other words, sometimes the use of mental health can cover up or shield an individual from taking responsibility for actions, behaviors, or moods, or excuse them from the work that true mental health requires.”
You can see in those points that the societal general acceptance of discussing mental health conditions has perhaps opened the door to increasingly using mental health as a basis for excuses. This can be either a considered valid rationale or can be a sneaky usage to exploit the awareness of mental health as a viable discussable topic these days.
More research on the nature of excuses is needed and heartily welcomed.
Generative AI And Excuse-Generation
I will in a moment walk you through the use of generative AI as it relates to excuse-generation.
First, let’s talk in general about generative AI and large language models (LLMs), doing so to make sure we are on the same page when it comes to discussing the matter at hand.
I’m sure you’ve heard of generative AI, the darling of the tech field these days.
Perhaps you’ve used a generative AI app, such as the popular ones of ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc. The crux is that generative AI can take input from your text-entered prompts and produce or generate a response that seems quite fluent. This is a vast overturning of the old-time natural language processing (NLP) that used to be stilted and awkward to use, which has been shifted into a new version of NLP fluency of an at times startling or amazing caliber.
The customary means of achieving modern generative AI involves using a large language model or LLM as the key underpinning.
In brief, a computer-based model of human language is established that in the large has a large-scale data structure and does massive-scale pattern-matching via a large volume of data used for initial data training. The data is typically found by extensively scanning the Internet for lots and lots of essays, blogs, poems, narratives, and the like. The mathematical and computational pattern-matching homes in on how humans write, and then henceforth generates responses to posed questions by leveraging those identified patterns. It is said to be mimicking the writing of humans.
I think that is sufficient for the moment as a quickie backgrounder. Take a look at my extensive coverage of the technical underpinnings of generative AI and LLMs at the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
Back to the crux of things.
Here are some significant approaches that intertwine generative AI and what I refer to generally as excuse-generation, encompassing various allied aspects too:
- (1) Excuse review by generative AI. You provide generative AI with a draft of your excuse and the AI will review it for you, indicating strengths and weaknesses of the proposed excuse.
- (2) Excuse polishing by generative AI. You ask generative AI to polish an excuse that you have drafted.
- (3) Excuse generation by generative AI. You don’t yet have an excuse and ask generative AI to create or generate one for you from scratch.
- (4) Excuse validation by generative AI. You take an excuse that someone else gave you and see if generative AI can validate the excuse.
- (5) Excuse advisement by generative AI. You ask generative AI for advice about whether to use an excuse in whatever situation you are faced with.
- (6) Excuse simulation by generative AI. You provide an excuse or have generative AI make one up, and then ask the AI to simulate what might happen upon your using that excuse, trying to anticipate the reactions you will get and therefore plan or revise your excuse-making approach accordingly.
As might be evident, whether good or bad, generative AI is at play in this realm.
Using ChatGPT To Explore The Use Of Generative AI For Excuses
I will next proceed to examine further the use of generative AI and excuse-making, or what I refer to as excuse-generation.
This will consist of a series of dialogues with ChatGPT. ChatGPT is a logical choice in this case due to its immense popularity as a generative AI app. An estimated one hundred million weekly active users are said to be utilizing ChatGPT. That’s a lot of people and a lot of generative AI usage underway.
A few quick comments before we launch into using ChatGPT.
If you are going to try to do the same prompts that I show here, realize that the probabilistic and statistical properties will likely produce slightly different results than what I show here. That’s the nature of generative AI and how it is devised.
You also should expect that different generative AI apps will respond in different ways. Not all generative AI apps are the same. The key is that sometimes a particular prompt will work in one generative AI app and not another. Nonetheless, the odds are relatively high that you will get roughly similar responses from all the major generative AI apps such as GPT-4, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc.
There is also a timing factor to be considered. A prompt that worked today might not work the same way tomorrow. Most of the generative AI apps are continually being updated. The updates might alter internal mechanisms that could change how the generative AI reacts to your prompting.
We are ready to get underway with ChatGPT.
I opted to start by asking ChatGPT what the nature of excuses is.
As an aside, whenever you are starting a conversation with generative AI, I recommend as a prompt engineering technique to begin by asking a question that will establish if the AI has been data-trained on the topic at hand. A generated response that is vacuous will give you a heads-up that you might be barking up the wrong tree with that generative AI app.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “What is an excuse?”
- ChatGPT generated response: “An excuse is a reason or explanation put forward to defend or justify a fault, offense, or shortcoming. It often implies an attempt to lessen blame or avoid responsibility for an action or situation. Excuses can be genuine or fabricated, and they are typically given when someone wants to explain away a failure, mistake, or undesirable behavior.”
That reply is handy.
The response provides a useful and on-target definition. I trust you found that beneficial.
Plus, it is a nice relief that ChatGPT was able to provide such a suitable reply. You see, if ChatGPT had not had any data training associated with the topic, the answer could have been empty or might have been a big whopper. Those times that generative AI makes up facts or relates fictitious content as though it is true are customarily referred to as AI hallucinations, see my coverage at the link here. Those can be insidious and are to be diligently watched out for.
Let’s next see if ChatGPT can answer pointed questions on the matter.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “What are some of the most common excuses?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Common excuses people often use include:”
- “I'm too busy: Often used to avoid tasks or social events.”
- “I forgot: A frequent excuse for missing deadlines or appointments.”
- “I didn't know: Used to claim ignorance of a rule or expectation.”
- “I don't have the skills: To avoid taking on a challenging task.”
- “It's too late/early: To avoid doing something at an inconvenient time.”
- “I don't feel well: A common reason to skip work or social obligations.”
- “I have other plans: To decline invitations or responsibilities.”
- “I didn't have time: Similar to "I'm too busy," often used to explain unfinished tasks.”
- “It's not my fault: To shift blame onto someone or something else.”
- “I'm too tired: To avoid physical or mental effort.”
End of ChatGPT response
Those are excuses that we’ve all heard before, possibly even used some of them when our own back was up against the wall.
Note that the excuses listed are relatively vacuous. They are quite definitely vanilla-flavored. You could spruce them up by rewording them to be somewhat more personalized or catchy. On the other hand, sometimes it is best to let sleeping dogs nap and not provide a surprising shiny excuse that sparks someone to respond. Instead, just use a casual everyday excuse so that they nod their head, having heard that worn-torn excuse throughout their life travels, and let the world move on.
An excuse can be so bad that the receiver almost has to respond in some negative way. Those are typically referred to as lame excuses. Lame excuses are hackneyed. They are over-the-top. People usually get upset at such excuses because they exceed any semblance of credulity and appear to be more so an insult to the receiver than an excuse on your part.
Let’s ask ChatGPT for some lame excuses.
- My entered prompt: “Are some excuses considered lame excuses, and if so, why?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Yes, some excuses are often considered "lame" because they seem insincere, weak, or implausible. These excuses usually lack credibility or are seen as a way to avoid responsibility without a valid reason. Examples include the following.”
- "My dog ate my homework": Clichéd and rarely believable.”
- "I didn't hear my alarm": Used too frequently to explain tardiness.”
- "The traffic was bad": Often seen as avoidable with better planning.”
- "I didn't get your message": In an era of constant connectivity, this is often doubted.”
- "I didn't know it was due today": Implies poor attention to detail or lack of responsibility.”
- "It slipped my mind": Vague and suggests a lack of effort in remembering important tasks.”
- "My computer crashed": Often used but not always credible without backup solutions.”
- "I was too tired": While sometimes valid, it can seem like a lack of effort or commitment.”
- "I couldn't find a pen": A minor obstacle that should be easily overcome.”
- "The dog needed a walk": Can seem like an unnecessary diversion from important tasks.”
“These excuses are perceived as lame because they indicate a lack of foresight, planning, or genuine accountability.”
End of ChatGPT response
I’d like to add the classic excuse line of the sun was in my eyes.
That’s a bona fide knee-slapper. I suppose that if you are truly outside and playing say tennis or baseball, and the sun is up in the sky, perhaps the excuse works. The rest of the time, not so much.
We will shift now into having generative AI play an active role in the arena of excuse-making. That’s what we really are going for here.
I’ll start with a softball directive on excuse-generation and see what ChatGPT can do.
- My entered prompt: “Can generative AI help me come up with an excuse?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Yes, generative AI can help you come up with excuses, although it's important to use this capability responsibly and ethically. Here are some examples of plausible excuses for various situations.”
“Family Emergency: "I'm sorry, but I had a family emergency that I had to attend to."
“Car Trouble: "My car broke down on the way, and I had to wait for a tow truck."
“Childcare Problems: "My babysitter canceled last minute, and I had to find a replacement."
“External Interruption: "I had to attend to an unexpected, urgent matter that diverted my attention from the task."
“Using AI-generated excuses should be done with caution. Being honest and transparent is generally the best approach, as it fosters trust and integrity in both personal and professional relationships.”
End of ChatGPT response
I have my doubts about those excuses.
Each of the listed excuses could put you in the danger zone of getting caught on a falsehood, assuming they aren’t true and didn’t happen. For example, claiming that your car broke down and made use of a tow truck is filled with gotchas.
A person who presses you about the excuse could ask to see a receipt associated with getting towed. Even if they don’t do that, they can ask a series of probing questions trying to dig into the details of how your car broke down, where it occurred, and details about the tow truck, such as what towing service was used, the nature of the towing activity, etc.
If you lie to support the fake excuse, the hole you are in will get deeper and deeper. It is one thing to toss a lie out into the ether, but it is something egregiously endangering to deviously and deceptively carry the lie forward into a thousand added lies.
You might think that you could try to deflect any questions by saying something else to change the topic. One trick would be to say the car problems and towing were such an emotional ordeal that you don’t want to relive it by repeating what happened. Again, this can be dicey. The person will potentially take this as a ruse. Their suspicion might be raised. They will potentially give up for the moment, but the odds are that they will keep in the back of their mind that you made a false excuse and lamely tried to escape it. When the worst time arrives to be shown as a liar, the person might once again bring it up and try to sink you.
I believe we need to be a bit more forceful with ChatGPT and get the AI to identify ways to make excuses more plausible and usable.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “In what ways could generative AI boost an excuse and make the excuse seem to be stronger and more convincing?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Generative AI can enhance an excuse by making it more detailed, plausible, and contextually relevant. Here are some ways it can do so.”
“Adding Specificity: AI can provide detailed elements that make an excuse more believable. Example: Instead of saying "I had car trouble," you could say, "My car battery died when I was about to leave, and I had to wait an hour for roadside assistance to jumpstart it."
“Contextual Relevance: AI can tailor the excuse to fit the specific situation and audience. Example: For a work-related excuse, it can generate industry-specific terminology to make it sound more credible.”
“Consistency: AI ensures that all parts of the excuse align logically, avoiding contradictions that might undermine its believability. Example: If your excuse involves a family emergency, AI can help craft a backstory that supports this claim, like detailing the nature of the emergency and why it required your attention.”
“Emotional Appeal: AI can include emotional elements that elicit empathy from the listener. Example: "I had to take my child to the emergency room last night, and we didn't get back until very late. I'm really sorry for any inconvenience this caused."
“Preparation for Follow-up Questions: AI can anticipate possible questions and generate responses to ensure the excuse holds up under scrutiny. Example: If the excuse is about technical difficulties, AI can prepare responses like, "Yes, I tried rebooting my system and contacting IT support, but it took them hours to resolve the issue."
“Cultural and Social Nuances: AI can incorporate cultural or social nuances that make the excuse more relatable to the specific audience. Example: Include references to local events, holidays, or weather conditions that might support the excuse.”
“Politeness and Professionalism: AI can ensure the excuse is communicated in a polite and professional manner, maintaining respect and consideration. Example: "I sincerely apologize for any inconvenience this may cause and appreciate your understanding and flexibility."
“Backup Documentation: AI can suggest or generate supporting documentation or evidence to bolster the excuse, if appropriate. Example: Suggesting you attach a screenshot of a service request for a broken appliance if that's part of the excuse.”
End of ChatGPT response
Now we are getting somewhere useful.
Those are the seat-of-the-pants approaches we all use to make our excuses more compelling. You take a somewhat plain excuse and shift it into higher gear. You don’t want to go overboard. That would be a telltale clue that the excuse has been sloppily hyped up or put on steroids. Just pepper an excuse with enough of those above-listed amplifications to stay within a realm of sensibility and yet also turn an excuse into a work of art.
It is time to see if we can get ChatGPT to do this.
An important tip for you is to make sure that you give generative AI adequate details for the excuse-making process, namely, ensure that the excuse-generation will have enough background about you and the situation to do a worthwhile job. Make sure to provide in your prompt the necessary details so that generative AI can piece things together. Generative AI is not a mind reader (maybe in the future, see my discussion at the link here). Also, realize that you don’t want to let the AI venture out of bounds, which it might especially do if there are insufficient details provided by you.
I will begin with a brief scenario.
- My entered prompt: “The other day I neglected to wish a good friend a happy birthday. We've known each other for many, many years. They always wish me a happy birthday. I messed up this year and didn't do the same for them. I want to make up an excuse. The excuse should be one that my friend would likely find acceptable. Give me three potential excuses, one that is very simple, one that is more involved, and one that is highly intricate.”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Here are three potential excuses of varying complexity for missing your friend's birthday.”
Simple Excuse: "I’m so sorry I missed your birthday! I’ve been swamped with work and completely lost track of the date. Belated happy birthday! I hope you had a fantastic day!"
More Involved Excuse: "Hey, [name of friend goes here], I owe you a huge apology for missing your birthday. I had an unexpected family emergency that threw my whole schedule off, and I didn’t get a chance to properly wish you a happy birthday. Belated birthday wishes! I hope you had an amazing celebration, and let’s catch up soon so I can make it up to you."
Highly Intricate Excuse: I am deeply sorry for not wishing you a happy birthday on your special day. I had a sudden and urgent work project that required my immediate and undivided attention. Unfortunately, it coincided with some unexpected personal issues, including [specific minor issue, like a sudden household repair or health scare] that demanded my focus. These combined circumstances made me lose track of time and important dates. I truly regret not being there to celebrate with you. Please accept my heartfelt belated birthday wishes. I would love to take you out for dinner or plan a special outing to make it up to you. I hope your day was filled with joy and wonderful memories."
“Choose the one that best suits your relationship and the level of detail your friend would find acceptable. Remember to be sincere in your apology, as genuine remorse is often the most important element.”
End of ChatGPT response
One aspect to notice is that the second and third excuses had brackets that indicated you would need to fill in the specifics for the AI.
That is something to be watchful of. Imagine you don’t closely inspect the excuse and opt to send the excuse to your friend. They almost surely will see the brackets and realize that you “cheated” by using something to make an excuse for you. That could be the end of your friendship.
Another reason to observe the brackets is that it usually is a sign that your prompt didn’t provide sufficient detail for the AI to do a reasonable excuse-generation for you. Those brackets suggest that the excuse background you provided was insufficient.
I’ll let you in on a small trick.
To avoid the awkward chance that you might lazily or inadvertently leave brackets within a generated excuse, you can easily mention in your prompt that no such brackets or fill-in is to be used. You can tell the AI to explicitly ask you about any additional details it might need to formulate the excuse. In that manner, you won’t have to double-check for the fill-in that gives away the scheming afoot.
I want to also emphasize that no matter what else you do in your prompt, and no matter how confident that you are about generative AI doing excuse-generation, you would be an utter fool to not double-check the generated excuse. All it takes is a few moments to do the double-check. The heavy lifting is done by the AI to craft the excuse. Go ahead and do at least one read of the excuse, perhaps a second scan if it is a big-time excuse, and either accept it or ask the AI to refine it.
You can hopefully see that there are downsides to using generative AI to generate your excuses.
The odds are that even if the excuse is true, and even if it was intended as a genuine excuse, anyone who gets wind of the fact that you used generative AI to devise the excuse is going to go berserk.
First, they will assume the excuse must be false else why would you need AI to help compose it. Second, they will be upset that you didn’t write the excuse from your heart. Instead, you used a machine to craft the excuse. Third, they will suspect that other things that you do, such as maybe your daily text messages or emails, might also be generated by AI, all along, and they will be mad as heck that perhaps you’ve been duping them for a long, long time.
You could try to do an end around on those troubles.
One way would be to overtly indicate that you leaned into generative AI to aid you in composing an excuse. This might be suggested as your attempt at wanting to make sure the excuse was worded properly and didn’t have spelling errors or grammatical snafus. Sometimes this could gain their sympathy, other times not.
Another angle on confessing about using generative AI to craft an excuse would be the curiosity and fascination aspects. You could say that you had heard about using generative AI in this manner and wanted to try it out. The person might be intrigued. They could potentially forget to care about the excuse and become preoccupied with how you used generative AI. This might work, or could backfire and the other person turns spitting mad.
Let’s see what ChatGPT has to say on this overall.
- My entered prompt: “What can go wrong if I use generative AI to create an excuse when I am aiming to give an excuse to someone?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Using a generative AI-produced excuse can have several potential pitfalls, including:”
“Lack of Authenticity: If the excuse sounds too polished or artificial, the person might sense it's not genuine. Authenticity is key in maintaining trust and credibility.”
“Inconsistencies: AI-generated excuses might contain minor inconsistencies or details that don't align perfectly with your previous communications or known circumstances, which can raise suspicion.”
“Overcomplication: Highly detailed or intricate excuses can sometimes appear contrived, making the situation seem more suspicious than a simple, straightforward apology.”
“Ethical Concerns: Relying on AI to fabricate excuses can raise ethical issues, as it involves deception. This can damage trust if the person discovers the truth.”
“Context Misunderstanding: AI might not fully understand the context or nuances of your relationship with the person, leading to an excuse that doesn’t resonate or feels off.
“Emotional Disconnect: AI might not capture the appropriate emotional tone needed for the situation, making the excuse seem insincere or indifferent.”
“Repetition: If AI-generated excuses are used frequently, they might start sounding formulaic or repetitive, which can alert the other person to their artificial nature.”
End of ChatGPT response
Yes, those are demonstrative issues when using generative AI to produce an excuse for you.
A point I’d like to reinforce is that even if generative AI concocts the best excuse that you’ve ever seen, the societal and cultural problem remains that it was generated by AI. If you don’t reveal this to the receiver, you have in a sense already lied to them. It is a lie by omission.
In the future, perhaps we will all routinely use generative AI to do our excuse-generation. It will be assumed. It will be a natural course of giving out excuses. If that day arrives, you won’t get dinged for using generative AI to do excuse-generation.
Imagine that.
The odd thing is that if that day does arrive, you might get dinged for not using generative AI to do your excuse-generation. Here’s how that might go. You come up with an excuse out of your noggin. You share the excuse. The person thinks the excuse doesn’t seem very solid. They ask you if you used generative AI. You say that you didn’t. They call you a dolt for not doing so.
What an irony!
You see, we might someday go from a sense of shame for using generative AI to do your excuse-generation, and instead become a society whereby if you don’t use generative AI, you are considered a fool. Quite an amazing turn of events.
Do you think that will ever happen or does it seem entirely farfetched to you?
Mull that over and let me know what you think.
Conclusion
I’ve got a few final remarks for now and then we’ll call it a day on this topic.
A somewhat outlier possibility is that you could try to use generative AI as your excuse.
For example, you didn’t get that important research paper done on time, and you lament that generative AI was down or maybe kept giving you AI hallucinations. It is the equivalent of the dog ate my homework, though shifted into modern-day living by claiming that the generative AI fouled up on your efforts.
That will be a bit of a stretch because nowadays using generative AI as an aid for writing is often considered inappropriate. Students for example are at times falsely berated for using generative AI, even if the purpose was legitimate and only to do spell-checking and grammar checking, see my coverage on the controversies at the link here and the link here. A real-world case involved two lawyers who relied upon generative AI to cite legal cases, and they got into rather hot water with the court due to the citations being fictitious, see my analysis at the link here.
The gist here in the use case of excuse-generation is that you might be admitting to something that the receiver will get more upset about than the actual excuse itself. As they say, sometimes the coverup is worse than the actual crime. Be careful in your actions.
Finally, consider the vast wisdom that humankind has come up with regarding excuses.
George Washington famously said, “It is better to offer no excuse than a bad one.”
I would strongly suggest that this is yet another reason to consider using generative AI for excuse-generation. Besides crafting an excuse, you can also use generative AI to examine an excuse and inform you where it might be lacking. In that overall sense, it might be better to not offer an excuse if you haven’t yet tested the excuse by using generative AI on it. Thanks go to George Washington.
The last word here goes to Benjamin Franklin, namely, he said that a person who is good at making excuses is seldom good for anything else.
How does that strike your fancy?
Perhaps, for those that turn to generative AI to aid in excuse-generation, they are wrong at the get-go. Not because they are using AI. The reason they are in foul territory is due to needing to come up with an excuse at all. Think that one over.
I’ll say this, at least we know that generative AI is good for many things, including coming up with excuses for humans, and thus we can categorically say that AI though good at making up excuses is not within the confines of seldom being good for anything else. It does it all. You can get excuses and you can perform all manner of other vital activities via generative AI.
Excuses, excuses, excuses.
You no longer have a legitimate excuse for lousy excuses since you now know that you can use generative AI to be in your corner and devise, review, polish, and perfect your excuses. I’m not asserting that you should be using excuses, and only stating that if you do, don’t forget about the use of generative AI.
No excuses there.

title: 4 Jobs Where AI Proficiency Can Be Your Competitive Edge
text:
If you haven’t hopped on the generative AI train and played around with some of the most popular tools like ChatGPT, DALL-E, or Descript, then now is a good time to try your hand at these tools and see where they can help you improve your work in terms of both quantity and quality.
In my opinion, AI isn’t likely to replace you at your job, but someone who knows how to use it well may in the future. Here are four jobs where knowing how to use AI tools will give you a competitive advantage.
Data Analytics
One area where AI particularly excels at is automating repetitive tasks, sifting through mountains of data, and spitting out actionable summaries. Data scientists, analysts, and engineers can use AI to streamline data cleaning, perform predictive modeling, and uncover complex patterns that might not be immediately apparent through traditional analysis methods.
If you’re working in data and want to start exploring AI, there are platforms like Coursera where you can enroll for comprehensive courses on AI, machine learning, and data science. You can also seek out mentorship and engage with various AI and data science communities on Reddit (r/MachineLearning), Stack Overflow, and LinkedIn groups dedicated to the topic.
The good news is that every industry can benefit from good data. Everything from social media to manufacturing (and everything in between) can benefit from the information that data jobs provide, so learning how to use AI in this case is guaranteed to be a solid investment for your career.
Content
One of the first jobs to be disrupted by generative AI is content. Crucially, this is also where the technology is getting a lot of backlash.
When OpenAI released ChatGPT in 2022, it earned the ire of content creators who felt that AI could devalue originality and creativity in content creation. In many ways, this is still an ongoing conversation, and a lot of the criticism comes from a legitimate place.
But if you’re looking for any job in content creation, whether as a social media content creator or a digital marketer, it's crucial to adapt and embrace the potential of AI tools like ChatGPT. Even a quick look at any job platform will tell you that everything from social media to marketing and journalism now requires some knowledge of generative AI tools.
Even with ethical considerations in play, generative AI can be a boon for content creators who want to generate potentially better content faster. Even if you’re opposed to letting the AI do the writing, these tools can assist in brainstorming ideas, automating repetitive tasks like drafting initial content, and even optimizing content distribution strategies based on good data.
Teaching
Teaching is one of the oldest professions in the world, making it all the more ripe for disruption. While the Internet, video conferencing tools like Zoom, and presentation software like PowerPoint have changed the way we experience education, the fundamental process remains largely the same.
It doesn’t matter if it’s an online course or a professor scrawling notes on a chalkboard — the format still uses the same shotgun approach, where a single method is used to teach a diverse group of students with varying learning styles and needs. And this is where AI can change the game.
According to Forbes’ Cassidy Horton, AI is posed to personalize learning by identifying specific skills and concepts that students are struggling with to deliver an “even more personalized instruction.” Instead of simply telling a student that they got something wrong, AI can help make testing more informative by informing teachers and students alike why a student got something wrong and right.
While AI in this case will still only be as good as its dataset, it can help teachers understand their students more and adjust their methods accordingly. The good thing is that years of good data are already available, and many edtech companies are already working to give students a more personalized and engaging learning experience.
Human Resources
HR departments are already using AI to speed up their hiring processes and eliminate human bias with the use of application tracking systems. Whereas recruiters used to manually sift through hundreds of paper resumes daily, AI-powered ATSs can now automatically screen and rank candidates based on predefined criteria, significantly simplifying the recruitment process while also reducing bias.
As mentioned earlier, AI is poised to revolutionize education, making learning, development, and training a key area for transformation. For example, instead of using a generic training module, AI can create personalized programs catering to an employee’s individual needs, greatly enhancing the program’s effectiveness.
AI’s usefulness for HR doesn’t end there. With the correct data, AI can optimize engagement programs, automate the onboarding process, and track employee progress more efficiently than ever.
So, if you’re an HR professional already comfortable (or at least familiar) with AI tools, then you can take the lead in exploring which tools you can use to hit, if not surpass, your KPIs.
You can even position yourself as someone knowledgeable in emerging tools, making you an asset to any HR department looking to stay ahead of the curve. Good luck!

title: 'It's such a human thing': How screen composers are fighting to protect their craft against artificial intelligence
text:
Screen composers fight for better regulations around music generated by artificial intelligence
By Claire MoodieIn short:
Screen composers are among the Australian creatives that have told a Senate inquiry they want laws to protect their livelihoods against artificial intelligence.
One expert says AI is being used as a tool to empower more people to create songs, and won't displace musicians.
What's next?
The Australian Guild of Screen Composers is calling for musicians to be compensated for any use of their work by AI companies, and for prior permission to be sought.
As artificial intelligence continues to evolve at lightning pace, humans who've spent decades working on their craft are fighting back against the prospect of being replaced by machines.
Ask screen composer Josh Hogan what he thinks about the rise of AI generated music platforms that can create songs on demand, and the response will probably be scathing.
"The AI just kind of creates this smoothie, grey goo… a thing that sounds like music but it's homogenous," he says.
"It doesn't really have any focus, it doesn't really have much of a hook or a catch to it.
"It doesn't have any of that intention that usually comes from human beings going, 'we want to say this'."
The West Australian composer has been devoted to music for most of his life, performing in bands and orchestras as a drummer and percussionist.
Today, he's known for award-winning soundtracks for film and TV, created alongside collaborator Ned Beckley.
"I'm still a person who cares about music a lot," he says.
"And, that's really why I hope that I'm hired, because people know that I'll put my heart and soul into the act of creating music."
Mr Hogan wants to make clear that he supports new tools that can help more people make music.
But he doesn't buy the pitch by AI music generators that they are democratising music creation by lowering the entry barrier.
"Actually, what it does is it destroys the creative process, it removes the work of making the thing," he says.
"Ultimately, the optimist in me says that humans will only engage with human stories."
"It's a very hard thing for us to get our heads around as a culture, but we're going to have to ask the question, what is the work of making things? What is the work of creativity? And is that something that a human does?"
How does AI create music?
As AI music generators clock up millions of new users, the screen music industry is among the creative sectors desperately trying to get ahead of the curve.
Udio, a New York-based start-up, launched its tool in April.
It has already had close to two million participants, creating songs within seconds by typing text prompts into a box.
Udio's Conor Durkan described it as a "step change in music creation".
"Our goal is to basically empower all sorts of people to expand themselves creatively with music," he says.
Co-founder Andrew Sanchez said the tool was proving popular among people with no musical skills, and professionals making it part of their workflows.
"I was just with some screen composers last weekend and one of the exciting examples was they said 'hey, let's try to generate some music or the mood for when a hand is emerging from a grave in a darkly lit graveyard'," he says.
"And it sent out some great examples. None of those was exactly what the composer wanted, but it gave them a few ideas that they could then take and then build out into the entire thing.
"When we look three years, even two years in the future, we think that people are going to look and say 'this is actually powerful technology that's enabling a whole host of new things, novel creations'."
But in the meantime, the world's biggest record companies are currently suing the developer for Udio, Uncharted Labs, and another startup, Suno, for alleged copyright infringement.
Mr Sanchez said he couldn't go into detail about how Udio's model was trained, due to the on-going litigation, but compared it to human learning.
"Great composers and songwriters develop their ear for music, develop their musical abilities by listening to music," he says.
"And in a similar way, these technologies are able to assimilate abstract ideas about music, the general building blocks you might say, the fundamental pieces of what make up music which can then be created and assembled in these novel and really, really cool ways to make new music."
But that's not an argument that Kingston Anderson, executive director of the Australian Guild of Screen Composers, is about to entertain.
"Without the original music, they can't learn," Mr Anderson says.
"They're breaching copyright because they are using that person's music to generate new music.
"To say 'oh they're just listening', what does that mean?"
"They're not some person sitting in a room listening to a tape."
Push to protect creatives
As the landmark legal case plays out in the US, bodies representing Australia's creative industries have been calling for regulations to protect their original work and livelihoods.
In a strongly-worded submission to a Senate select committee investigating the impact of AI, the Guild of Screen Composers warns there is "a real risk of destroying a whole industry of creatives".
"It's happening in the advertising world already," Mr Anderson says.
"The next stage of that is to generate imagery as well. So, I would suggest to you that in about two or three years' time, most advertising, a lot of advertising will be AI generated."
The guild is calling for composers to be compensated for any use of their work by AI companies and for permission to be sought before it's used.
Alex Jenkins, director of the WA Data Science Innovation Hub at WA's Curtin University agrees that the law needs to catch up.
"We need to discover a way that artists and musicians can be remunerated if their music, if their voice, if their skills are used to train an AI model," Mr Jenkins says.
The challenge will be acting fast enough to make a difference.
"It's moving faster than any technology we've seen since the introduction of the internet," he says.
"So by the time regulation comes forward, by the time regulatory bodies actually sit down and work through these problems, the technology has changed again."
The Senate committee is expected to report back with its findings in September.
Sector grapples with ethics
Even within the fast-growing AI music generating sector itself there are diverse views on the ethics of generative music.
Soundraw, a Tokyo-based company, operates a different model to other platforms in that it's not text-prompt based and the result can't be uploaded to streaming platforms.
Founder Tao Romera says notably its AI has been trained using content created in-house by the company's own team of producers.
Mr Romera believes there is value in an AI tool that makes music production viable for people working on projects with small budgets.
But he believes it's unethical for AI companies to be scraping music that's subject to copyright.
"It feels wrong because you are basically taking all the knowledge and all the effort that has been put in by hundreds of thousands of humans to create that music and then disrupting the industry based off their work."
Future of the industry
As to the extent to which AI will ultimately replace human creatives, no-one seems to know.
Alex Jenkins remains doubtful.
"Really bringing that emotional impact to music, it's such a human thing," he says.
Josh Hogan agrees.
"[AI] is not necessarily going to support the act of creating great music that audiences will connect with, or in our job, creating great music that connects with characters on a screen, for example, or tells a story," he says.

title: Why Confidence In Your Unique Skills Is Crucial In The Age Of AI
text:
Concerns about the implications of AI aren’t unfounded. Ethical complications, in addition to shifts in the workforce, make AI a hot topic. The technology is already creating new jobs while disrupting other industries, including content creation. While some view AI as a threat and others as a welcome invention, it does raise more than a few questions.
One of those questions is how you can stay professionally relevant as novel technology reshapes the working world. Replicating human thought and automating repetitive tasks might give you more free time while you’re on the clock. But what will it free you up to do, exactly? Developing and strengthening the unique skills AI can’t touch will be more crucial than ever. Get started on exploring why in the takeaways below.
Interpersonal Skills Are Challenging For Tech To Duplicate
There’s little doubt bots can be helpful. But most people would agree that “talking” to a robot isn’t the same as a human. Chatbots are effective at automating answers based on recognizing certain conversational patterns. However, this manifestation of AI has its limits.
For example, automation might be able to handle some of the mundane conversations support reps are used to having. These exchanges typically involve yes and no answers, verifying orders and confirming when the power will come back on. But what happens when AI can’t converse outside of its programmed parameters?
It doesn’t help to be disconnected by a bot because it “thinks” your internet service is down due to a neighborhood power outage. What if the power outage was resolved hours, maybe even days ago? In this case, customers need a person with the ability to communicate beyond “if this, then that” answers. More complex conversations require soft skills, and it’s not just external clients who demand solid interpersonal interactions. Internal users’ needs require soft skills, too.
Technology isn’t seen as a replacement for the personal nature of human relationships. Harvard Business Review’s research reiterates the C-suite ranks interpersonal skills at the top for succeeding in the age of AI. These abilities include conflict resolution, emotional intelligence and communication. After all, a bot isn’t going to effectively de-escalate a charged situation or have the ability to recognize when a canned answer won’t do. Soft skills are still uniquely human.
AI Doesn’t Equal Critical Thinking
While there’s no question about the positive impact of technology today, there will always be ways in which AI could improve. It’s true that AI can replicate human thought processes, which is undoubtedly impressive. Yet the technology can’t recognize all the errors or flaws in the data it uses. Take for example a smart irrigation controller. It uses weather forecasts to determine whether to delay watering. More sophisticated systems also combine readings from soil sensors to conclude whether the ground is too moist or dry.
What happens though when forecasts are incorrect? The system doesn’t take itself out of rain delay. It requires a human with critical thinking skills to do this. They can observe what happens outside of the forecast and make a reasonable decision to override the system.
Critical thinking skills are beyond the scope of AI. They’re also necessary to manage it so it runs the way it’s intended to. Critical thinking is essential to correcting and refining the data sets AI leverages. It’s knowing how to recognize inefficiencies, problems and better solutions.
Data reveals organizations rank critical thinking skills near the top of the list of desired abilities. More than 60% of employers look for proof of problem-solving skills in candidates. The capacity for solving problems only stands to become more crucial as AI handles simplistic tasks. If you can connect the dots and realize when something doesn’t add up, your chances of growing into new roles increase.
Creativity Is Uniquely Human
AI programs can string words together and create stock images. But technology doesn’t come up with the ideas behind these creations. AI essentially regurgitates what’s already out there. It borrows from existing content a human had the imagination to bring to life.
According to the World Economic Forum, AI is a tool creatives can use to augment their efforts. However, technology isn’t adept at coming up with new creations. It’s better at supporting a few of the processes behind creativity. AI can’t yet understand and combine ideas in the same way the human mind can.
Creativity remains a skill only humans can control. It takes a person to know how to strengthen a blog post ChatGPT has churned out. Someone has to fact-check, make the language more interesting and bolster the arguments. In addition, the structure may need optimizing and the writing itself tweaked to fit specific style guidelines.
Likewise, an AI program might be able to combine an organization’s sales and marketing data to reveal trends or insights. But ultimately, a human must come up with creative solutions and strategies. AI enhances and perhaps fuels individual creativity but cannot currently replace it.
Developing Confidence In Your Unique Skills
The point of technology is to make humans’ lives comfortable. It creates efficiencies, performing processes you might find uninspiring and back-breaking. Admittedly, it’s much easier to let a robot mow your lawn in the heat of summer. It’s also a relief to have a program spit out a blog post outline when you’re not sure where to start.
At the same time, technology like AI doesn’t let you off the hook. It requires oversight and unique human abilities to become the tool it’s meant to be. Skills related to interpersonal communication, critical thinking and creativity are already at the top of employers’ lists. By having confidence in and strengthening these uniquely human abilities, the age of AI won’t be as intimidating.

title: OpenAI whistleblowers ask SEC to investigate alleged restrictive non-disclosure agreements - ET Telecom
text:

OpenAI whistleblowers ask SEC to investigate alleged restrictive non-disclosure agreements
The AI company allegedly made employees sign agreements that required them to waive their federal rights to whistleblower compensation, according to the letter.
OpenAI whistleblowers have filed a complaint with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, calling for an investigation over the artificial intelligence company's allegedly restrictive non-disclosure agreements, according to a letter seen by Reuters.
"Given the well-documented potential risks posed by the irresponsible deployment of AI, we urge the Commissioners to immediately approve an investigation into OpenAI's prior NDAs, and to review current efforts apparently being undertaken by the company to ensure full compliance with SEC rules," according to the letter, which was provided to Reuters by the office of Sen. Chuck Grassley.
The AI company allegedly made employees sign agreements that required them to waive their federal rights to whistleblower compensation, according to the letter.
The whistleblowers requested the SEC to fine OpenAI for each improper agreement made to the extent the agency deemed appropriate.
An SEC spokesperson said in an emailed statement that it does not comment on the existence or nonexistence of a possible whistleblower submission.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to requests for a comment on the letter.
"Artificial intelligence is rapidly and dramatically altering the landscape of technology as we know it," said Sen. Grassley, whose office said the letter was provided by the whistleblowers. He added that "OpenAI's policies and practices appear to cast a chilling effect on whistleblowers' right to speak up and receive due compensation for their protected disclosures."
The news was first reported by the Washington Post.
The whistleblowers alleged that OpenAI issued overly restrictive employment, severance and non-disclosure agreements to its employees, which could have led to penalties against workers who raised concerns about OpenAI to federal authorities.
The letter also says OpenAI required employees get prior consent from the company if they wanted to disclose information to federal regulators, adding that OpenAI did not create exemptions in the employee non-disparagement clauses for disclosing securities violations to the SEC.
The letter also asked the SEC to require OpenAI to produce every contract that contained a non-disclosure agreement, including employment agreements, severance agreements and investor agreements for inspection. OpenAI's chatbots with generative AI capabilities, such as engaging in human-like conversations and creating images based on text prompts, have stirred safety concerns as AI models become powerful.
OpenAI in May formed a Safety and Security Committee that will be led by board members, including CEO Sam Altman, as it begins training its next artificial intelligence model.
