title: Council Post: The Future Of Retail: Trends To Watch In The Second Half Of 2024
text:
Paul Lin, tech entrepreneur and CEO of Returned.com, dedicated to revolutionizing the retail returns process through innovative AI.
Retail technology is rapidly reshaping how businesses interact with customers and manage operations. As the CEO of Returned.com, I've witnessed firsthand the transformative power of technology in retail. With two decades of experience in tech-retail, including over 4 million Amazon transactions resulting in $300 million in sales, I've developed a deep understanding of the challenges and opportunities in this space.
My career journey, including leading Returned.com, has provided me with unique perspectives on leveraging technology to create impactful retail experiences. Here, I'll share my insights to help fellow technology professionals and retail leaders thrive.
1. Omnichannel Experiences
Consumers increasingly expect seamless shopping experiences across multiple channels, compelling retailers to integrate their online and offline operations. According to industry experts, 73% of consumers use many channels, and retailers using three or more channels see a 251% increase in customer engagement compared to single-channel retailers.
• Unified Customer Data: Integrating customer data from various channels allows retailers to create a single view of the customer, enabling personalized marketing and improved customer service.
• Consistent Branding: Unifying your messaging across channels helps build trust and recognition among consumers.
• Seamless Transitions: Technologies like QR codes, mobile apps and in-store kiosks can help bridge the gap between online and offline shopping.
2. Artificial Intelligence And Personalization
AI continues to revolutionize retail by enabling highly personalized shopping experiences. AI-driven personalization allows businesses to analyze large volumes of data to offer tailored product recommendations, marketing campaigns and optimized inventory management.
• Product Recommendations: AI algorithms analyze customer behavior and preferences to suggest products that are most likely to interest them.
• Dynamic Content: Personalized content, such as tailored emails and website banners, can be generated in real time based on individual customer data.
• Inventory Optimization: AI helps retailers predict demand and manage inventory more effectively.
3. Social Commerce And Live Commerce
Social media platforms are becoming significant sales channels, with live commerce emerging as a powerful trend. Social commerce, which involves selling products during broadcasts, has seen substantial growth.
• Interactive Shopping: Live commerce allows customers to interact with hosts and ask questions in real time.
• Influencer Partnerships: Collaborating with influencers can help retailers reach a wider audience and build credibility.
• Shoppable Posts: Social media platforms are integrating shopping features, allowing users to purchase products directly from posts and stories.
4. Sustainability, Eco-Friendly Practices And Donations
Sustainability is becoming a critical factor for consumers, who are increasingly demanding eco-friendly options and sustainable practices from retailers.
• Eco-Friendly Packaging And Sourcing: Using biodegradable, recyclable or reusable packaging materials and sourcing products from suppliers adhering to sustainable practices can significantly reduce environmental impact.
• Carbon Neutral Initiatives: Some retailers are committing to carbon neutrality by offsetting their carbon emissions through various environmental projects.
• Donate What Doesn’t Sell: Retailers can save money and time by donating unsellable inventory to nonprofits and schools.
5. Augmented Reality (AR) And Virtual Reality (VR)
AR and VR technologies are transforming the shopping experience by allowing customers to visualize products in real-world contexts.
• Virtual Try-Ons: AR apps allow customers to try on clothes, accessories and makeup virtually.
• Interactive Showrooms: Customers can explore products in virtual 3D showrooms in VR.
• Enhanced Product Visualization: AR can overlay product information and reviews in real time.
6. Voice Commerce And Conversational AI
Voice assistants and conversational AI are becoming significant trends in retail, allowing customers to place orders and receive personalized recommendations using voice commands.
• Voice Search Optimization: Retailers are optimizing their websites and product listings for voice search.
• Personalized Voice Assistants: AI-powered voice assistants can provide personalized shopping recommendations.
• Seamless Transactions: Voice commerce enables customers to complete transactions using voice commands.
7. Subscription Commerce
Subscription commerce has gained significant traction, with more retailers offering subscription-based models to provide convenience, personalization and value to customers.
• Personalized Subscriptions: Retailers use AI to offer highly personalized subscription boxes based on individual preferences.
• Replenishment Models: Subscription models are particularly suited for products that need regular replenishment.
• Exclusive Access: Some retailers offer exclusive access to limited-edition products or early releases through subscription models.
8. Smart Shipping And Data-Driven Logistics
The rise of smart shipping and data-driven logistics is optimizing the delivery process, reducing costs and enhancing efficiency.
• Real-Time Tracking: Advanced tracking systems provide real-time updates on the status of shipments.
• Automated Warehousing: AI-powered robots and automated systems are streamlining warehouse operations.
• Predictive Logistics: AI can predict potential delays and disruptions in the supply chain.
9. Enhanced Security And Privacy Measures
With the increasing use of AI and data analytics, ensuring the security and privacy of customer data is more important than ever.
• Data Encryption: Implementing strong encryption methods to protect customer data.
• Fraud Detection: AI algorithms can detect and prevent fraudulent activities.
• Privacy Policies: Clear and transparent privacy policies help build trust with customers.
10. Optimizing Returns Management
Efficient returns management is vital for customer satisfaction and operational efficiency.
• Predictive Analytics: AI analyzes historical data to predict likely returns.
• Automated Processing: Machine learning automates tasks like return authorization and refunds.
• Fraud Detection: AI detects fraudulent return activities.
Conclusion
The retail landscape in the second half of 2024 will be shaped by technological advancements and changing consumer expectations. Retailers that embrace these trends and invest in the necessary technologies will be well-positioned to thrive. From omnichannel experiences and AI-driven personalization to social commerce and sustainability, the future of retail promises to be exciting and full of opportunities.
Based on my experience, I recommend starting with a clear strategy for integrating new technologies, ensuring robust data security measures and seeking customer feedback to refine and enhance the shopping experience. By staying ahead of these trends and implementing best practices, businesses can create exceptional shopping experiences, drive growth and maintain a competitive edge.

title: Council Post: Why GRC Teams Should Take A 'Yes, And' Approach To AI
text:
Matt Kunkel is CEO of LogicGate, a GRC process automation platform that enables organizations to transform risk and compliance programs.
“Yes, and…” is a principle that originated in improv comedy but has become common in other contexts. The idea is simple: telling someone “no” can grind a situation to an awkward and uncomfortable halt, whether that situation is a comedy sketch or a corporate brainstorming session.
It’s better (and more productive) to roll with new ideas as they emerge, working together rather than against one another to build a stronger, more compelling result. That doesn’t mean every idea is a good one, but this approach at least provides the opportunity to fully examine a proposal rather than simply rejecting it. Who knows? Sometimes, talking through a bad idea can lead to something better.
This is particularly true for governance, risk and compliance (GRC) teams, who are often viewed as the “Department of No.” GRC teams look at everything through the lens of risk, and it can be easy to dismiss new ideas because they appear “too risky.” However, as technology like artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly widespread, saying no isn’t always an option.
While AI has its risks, the technology has the potential to revolutionize the way modern businesses operate—which means failing to adopt it might be the biggest risk of all. Rather than saying “no” to new AI tools, GRC teams should instead look for ways to say, “Yes, and…here’s how we can limit the risk.”
Why Saying “No” Is Not An Option
As useful as AI promises to be, the potential risks it brings with it are very real. Businesses must account for the security concerns surrounding AI, as well as the potential for legal, regulatory and even ethical roadblocks. It’s important to understand the organization’s overall risk tolerance and have a plan in place to address potential issues like data security, bias management and intellectual property rights.
With that in mind, it’s tempting for GRC teams to simply bar the use of AI tools until those questions have been addressed more thoroughly.
But in the real world, that isn’t really an option. AI is a (if not the) top initiative for every CFO in the nation right now. It’s the number one topic at industry conferences. It’s the first question at every board meeting. AI-based solutions are helping businesses streamline their reporting, improve their approach to communications, automate cumbersome manual processes and more. Work that used to take weeks or months can now be done in a day—and that has a huge impact on an organization’s bottom line.
If your business isn’t adopting AI, you can be sure your competitors are—and you risk being left behind. GRC teams can’t just say “no,” but there are steps organizations can take to make it easier (and safer) to say “yes.”
Embracing AI While Limiting Risk
Fortunately, today’s businesses don’t need to start from scratch. Advisory bodies like the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have already issued detailed frameworks that can help organizations better determine how much risk they are willing to take on—and how to manage it.
This often starts with understanding where AI is already being used within your organization—because if you don’t think employees are already using tools like ChatGPT, you’re fooling yourself. It’s impossible to manage a technology if you don’t know where it’s being used, so discovery must be a priority.
The organization can then begin establishing acceptable use policies for AI, which will ultimately be based on risk appetite. Is the business willing to accept the risks that come along with using AI for product development? Is there a clear process for determining what data can be fed into generative AI tools? Can AI solutions be protected using the company’s existing security solutions? If not, what will it take to secure them, and how much will it cost? These are questions that GRC teams need to be asking and discussing with their C-suite.
The answers to these questions will allow GRC teams to determine how they can say “yes, and…” rather than “no” to AI implementations. Yes, there are risks associated with AI in product development, and here’s how we can mitigate them. Yes, there are data protection policies in place, and here’s how they can be applied to AI. Yes, we need additional security solutions, and here are our recommendations.
By adopting this approach, the GRC department can become a helpful ally for stakeholders looking to increase their AI investments rather than a frustrating roadblock. Ultimately, it’s not just about avoiding risk—it’s about equipping business leaders with the information they need to make risk-conscious decisions that move the business forward.
That said, AI policies are only as effective as your ability to enforce them. That means businesses need to create a culture of transparency and risk awareness, ensuring that employees understand the rules and why they are in place.
Additionally, GRC teams need continuous visibility across the digital landscape, along with the ability to measure how effectively the organization is aligned with established frameworks. This also applies to third-party risk—at a time when businesses are being compromised through partners and vendors at a worrying rate, it’s critical to ensure that third-party organizations are also in compliance with GRC policies. After all, you’re only as secure as your weakest link.
The Need For A “Yes, and…” Approach
No technology is perfect, and AI is certainly no exception. But as AI becomes more widely adopted, more and more organizations will find that they are willing to accept the risk it carries in exchange for the business outcomes it drives.
And that’s fine. A good GRC team shouldn’t be the Department of No. They should work with stakeholders not to forbid the use of AI but to help them understand how it can be used safely and effectively, driving the business forward without exposing it to unnecessary risk.
AI is a game-changer for organizations across every industry, and embracing a “yes, and…” approach allows GRC teams to generate positive business outcomes while keeping drawbacks to a minimum.

title: No, Autism Is Not Caused By The Gut Microbiome
text:
Last week, the New York Times published a story claiming that we might be able to use the gut microbiome to diagnose autism. The Times story was based on a just-published scientific paper that claimed the same thing.
This report set off all my skeptical alarm bells. My initial reaction was “oh no, more bad science around autism.” For one thing, as most scientists studying autism are aware, the modern anti-vaccine movement started with a scientific paper, back in 1998, that claimed, falsely, that childhood vaccines caused autism. That paper in The Lancet was later shown to be fraudulent and was eventually retracted, but not before a huge amount of damage was done. Its lead author, Andrew Wakefield, went on to become a hero to the anti-vaccine movement, and he continues to promote anti-vaccine misinformation to this day.
The new paper (from the journal Nature Microbiology) is not making outrageous claims like that, nor was the New York Times. However, anyone claiming autism is caused by microbes in the gut should know that the notorious Lancet study was based on a hypothesis about a “leaky gut,” a hypothesis that was discredited long ago. (I don’t want to give it any credibility, but that hypothesis held that virus particles in some vaccines somehow “leaked” from the gut and made their way to the brain. It was nonsense at the time and still is.) That’s one reason why the suggestion that microbes in the gut might cause autism (or even be used to diagnose it) raises so many alarm bells.
I’ve now looked at the study, and frankly I don’t believe a word of it. Let me be clear, though: I’m not trying to prove scientifically that the study is wrong, which would require many months of effort and a much more detail than I can put into a column anyway. Fortunately, though, there’s an earlier study that did that job for me, which I’ll get to below.
However, the science behind this study is closely related to my own work, so I feel pretty comfortable offering my opinion. So what did the authors do?
Well, as the new study explains, they collected poop (”faecal samples”) from 1,627 children, some of whom had been diagnosed with autism and some who hadn’t, and they sequenced DNA from the poop. Then they looked for bacteria, viruses, and other microbes in the DNA sequence data.
That’s right: the “gut microbiome,” is really just a polite term for bacteria that live in the intestines and the colon, some of which come out in poop. Of course, some bacteria in poop might come from the food that a person ate, but mostly these are so-called gut bacteria.
I’ve been involved in many studies like this myself, so I’ve seen that these experiments yield hundreds of different species from every sample. The data sets are very complex, and a widespread problem in the field is that these data are often misinterpreted. In the Nature Microbiology paper, the authors took these very complex data sets and fed them to a machine learning program, and voila! The AI program was able to do a pretty good job (far from perfect, I should note) identifying the autistic children, based on the melange of microbes in their poop.
Right. I don’t believing any of this, as I wrote above. Why not? Well, first of all, machine learning programs are really good at telling apart two sets of subjects (such as children with and without autism) if you give them enough data. It sometimes turns out that the learning programs are keying in on irrelevant features that the scientists didn’t intend.
For example, this 2021 paper looked at over 400 studies that used machine learning to predict Covid-19, all of which had claimed some success, and found that all of the studies were essentially useless “due to methodological flaws and/or underlying biases.” Of course, the gut microbiome study wasn’t one of those, and some machine learning experiments do work, but we should be very skeptical.
Another reason for skepticism is that the new paper doesn’t even try to tell us what the machine learning models actually learned–it just treats the programs as a “black box” that we should trust.
Perhaps the biggest flaw in the study of autism and children’s gut microbiota is this: children with autism tend to be finicky eaters, and their parents try all sorts of diets in the hope that they can at least alleviate the symptoms of autism with food. There are countless websites–many of them scams, unfortunately–claiming that special diets can help these children. Why is this important? Because a special diet will alter your gut microbiome, sometimes quite significantly.
Thus even if the machine learning models in the new study are correct, the causality almost certainly goes the other way: children with autism might have a different microbiome because they’re eating different foods. Thus it’s autism that indirectly affects the microbiome. Unfortunately, both the New York Times and the scientific paper suggested the opposite.
Now on to that earlier scientific paper I mentioned above. It turns out 3 years ago, a group of researchers in Australia published a major study in the journal Cell that addressed precisely the problem I just pointed out. In that study, the scientists collected and sequenced poop from 247 children both with and without autism. They found “negligible direct associations between ASD [autism spectrum disorder] and the gut microbiome.“
On the contrary, the authors warned: “microbiome differences in ASD may reflect dietary preferences ... and we caution against claims that the microbiome has a driving role in ASD.”
In other words, three years ago a study in a major scientific journal found that there was no connection between autism and the contents of the gut microbiome. They went on to warn that if you see differences in the gut microbiome in autistic kids, those are caused by their diet, so don’t go claiming that the microbiome causes autism. The authors of the newer study, and the reporters at the New York Times, apparently decided otherwise.
So no, the gut microbiome can’t be used to diagnose autism.

title: From 'Don't Be Evil' To Legal AI: Tackling Bias And Complacency
text:
With the expansion of technology and AI into our daily lives, Edmund Burke's quote remains pertinent: "The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing."
Google's original motto, "Don't Be Evil," reflected good intentions. However, by 2018, changes in technology, strategic opportunities, and company size (with the accompanying ‘I’m just doing my job’ attitude), along with legal challenges, made it difficult for Google to adhere to these intentions - and the motto was dropped.
Similarly, the legal sector has experienced significant shifts due to technological advancements and changing strategic opportunities and threats. An example of these effects occurred in 2023, when US lawyers were sanctioned for using ChatGPT without verifying its output, leading to fictitious cases being cited in a legal brief.
Automation Bias & Complacency
Beyond the propensity of large language models to hallucinate, this incident highlights a broader issue for lawyers and other knowledge workers: automation bias and automation complacency, and their relationship to responsibility and ethics.
Automation bias is the tendency to trust technology unquestioningly, even when faced with contradictory evidence, while automation complacency arises when users trust machines without considering whether the machine’s output is correct.
The biases and complacency that plague human behavior stem from inherent cognitive, psychological, and motivational factors. These biases have become deeply embedded within the bureaucracies and organizations we have built over the course of human history. Attempting to remove the established processes and norms that allow the questioning of these biases is, therefore, hard.
Canaries in the Coal Mine
The legal industry is particularly vulnerable to automation bias and complacency. As Jose Alberto Lopez, co-founder of Vizlegal, notes, "the legal sector has been slower than others in adopting technology. Yet, given its emphasis on knowledge-based tasks, it's arguably one of the sectors most profoundly impacted by AI advancements.”
In a discussion with Lopez, whose company Vizlegal aggregates public legal data into accessible formats for legal firms, and Giles Slinger from Fledger.ai, whose software gives legal teams accurate insights faster from lengthy documents, we explored how the legal sector is at the forefront of transitioning to a knowledge-based economy—and the implications of this shift.
Lawyers are the "canaries in the coal mine" for knowledge work. As Slinger explains, “Lawyers are devices for turning information into answers. They are highly vulnerable to machines getting these answers more quickly. The lawyer’s added value is going to be legal accuracy, delivered with empathy.”
Considering, according to Slinger and Lopez, that lawyers spend at least 20% of their time finding information, AI represents a significant shift for the legal profession, making automation bias and complacency substantial threats. As in many industries, AI research and other capabilities are likely to replace junior staff who normally would be tasked with time consuming, but lower value, work. There is an assumption that younger, digital-native generations are better at using new tools, and at discerning fake from real information, thus guarding against automation bias, but evidence supporting this is scant. So, what does this mean for digital natives entering the workforce?
Hallucinating Large Language Models
Currently, AI's limitations, such as LLM hallucinations mentioned above, hinder full automation. Lawyers still need to verify cases cited by LLMs, which is why more legal tech firms are currently focusing on aggregating and searching existing data than on generating new data.
So, are there reasons for employing staff to do tasks that are likely to be accomplished by AI? According to Slinger “It has never been more important for senior partners to learn from how the 1st and 2nd year juniors are doing their work.” Staff who have the critical thinking skills to avoid automation bias combined with an understanding of how to use automation tools will be invaluable in changing how lawyers, and other sectors, work.
As a result, for law firms to compete and thrive today, they need a mix of technical innovation (AI), human critical thinking and the ability to argue and explain complex issues - a blend of youth from junior staff and wisdom from senior colleagues.
Where AI and Ethics Collide
Slinger highlights the increasing length of contracts in the legal arms race: “The arms race between lawyers means that contracts are getting longer, not shorter, as each lawyer finds it easier to add rather than remove clauses. Contracts that were 30 pages are now 70.” Longer contracts have been an issue even before AI, but as Slinger continues; “With an AI tool, at almost no cost, stronger claims can be added, new lines of attack explored. If the other side is not using AI, it is a free win. So the AI arms race grows exponentially.”
This is just one example of where AI dominance can creep. Thereafter, if lawyers (and other knowledge workers) are not vigilant against automation bias and complacency - greater responsibility is handed to AI. But AI does not have ethics, therefore by devolving responsibility, we are also subjugating ethics to AI as well.
Ensuring that employees take responsibility for the output of AI is not an easy problem to solve but ultimately comes back to creating a culture of trust and increasing the emphasis on soft skills including, but not limited to, critical thinking.
In last month’s Forbes article I covered the work of Alex Edmans who showed that investing in companies listed in the top 100 places to work provides better returns than following the index. These companies encourage pro-activeness and accountability - which can lead to critical thinking. This is required to create environments where doing nothing is not acceptable. Without this, unwittingly, we may be doing evil.

title: Council Post: How To Prepare Employees For AI-Enhanced Roles And Responsibilities
text:
Dr. Shay David is Co-founder and CEO of retrain.ai, an AI-Talent Intelligence Platform that uses skills to help hire faster & retain longer.
As technology has evolved, particularly in HR, its primary focus has been automation—streamlining repetitive tasks or processes to enhance efficiency. But in today's landscape, the new goal is augmentation driven by AI. Businesses are leveraging these tools to enhance human capabilities. For example, in customer service, chatbots handle basic queries, allowing human agents to address more-complex issues that require empathy and nuanced judgment.
AI's capabilities are creating a seismic shift in the labor market, and new job roles are emerging to support implementation and oversight. Roles like AI trainers, data ethicists and automation specialists are becoming vital for ensuring responsible AI deployment. As a result, professionals need support preparing for these new responsibilities.
Over the last few years, while building Retrain.ai, I’ve had the unique opportunity to witness the profound transformation that AI is bringing to the HR field and the employee experience. Through collaboration with various clients, I've gleaned valuable insights and seen inspiring examples of how augmented HR tech can revolutionize the workplace.
4 Strategies To Prepare Employees For AI-Enhanced Roles
There are a few ways HR leaders can ensure their organizations are preparing employees for the AI-powered future of work. Here are four approaches.
Focus On Upskilling And Reskilling
According to LinkedIn Learning's 2024 Workplace Learning report, 80% of employees want AI skills training. To prepare them, organizations must adopt comprehensive reskilling and upskilling initiatives. This can help ensure the workforce can effectively capitalize on AI technologies.
One strategy for upskilling is providing access to courses and certifications that train professionals in emerging technologies. Amazon’s Upskilling 2025 initiative is a prime example of a successful reskilling program. The corporation committed $700 million to upskill 100,000 employees for high-demand roles in areas like cloud computing and machine learning. The initiative includes programs like Amazon Technical Academy and Machine Learning University, which provide employees with the skills needed to transition to these roles.
Provide A Platform For Learning
Organizations should give employees access to a skills platform with personalized learning paths, progress tracking and relevant course suggestions. Providing a wide range of courses and resources will help employees stay current with industry trends. The right platform identifies skills gaps within an organization, allowing for targeted training initiatives that address specific needs.
Leveraging learning management systems can be key here because they make learning accessible and convenient, fitting into employees' busy schedules. Incorporating microlearning techniques—delivering bite-sized, easily digestible training modules—helps employees learn and retain information more effectively. This can allow them to fit learning into daily routines, ensuring continuous skill development.
Emphasize Soft Skills
There are many indispensable human traits that AI can't easily replicate, such as soft skills like adaptability, creativity and emotional intelligence. In fact, according to Salary.com's 2023 Skills Pulse Survey, the top three skills in demand are effective communication, problem-solving and critical thinking. Therefore, organizations should treat these as integral parts of employee development programs.
Keep Role Responsibilities And Competencies Up To Date
Workplace planning is essential in the rapidly changing skills landscape, so maintaining a modern, dynamic role catalog is a must. Aligning job roles with the necessary skills and competencies for today's workforce ensures employees understand the expectations and requirements of their positions. This aids in their professional growth and development in the age of AI integration.
The Role Of Continuous Learning As AI Evolves
Creating a culture of learning is paramount in today's fast-paced job market. Providing opportunities for regular skill assessments and personalized development plans can foster an environment where employees treat learning as a lifetime journey. This ensures they're always ready to adapt to new roles and technologies. By focusing on these strategies, organizations can successfully ensure their workforces are equipped to thrive in an AI-enhanced future.

title: Council Post: 6 Considerations For A School District’s AI Strategy
text:
Al Kingsley is CEO of NetSupport, Chair of a multi-academy trust in the U.K, tech writer, speaker and author of multiple education books.
Since bursting into the public domain in November 2022—albeit here for many years—artificial intelligence (AI) has found its way into practically every sector, and education is no exception. This is a space where workloads are heavy, demands are high and the pressure is constant. What better circumstances for AI to help with some of the heavy lifting?
What can AI do in schools?
Over the last 18 months, educators have been experimenting with various (now well-known) generative AI tools for text, images and more, finding that they can have a significant impact—not just on their workload but also on their students’ learning.
AI’s versatility and scope mean that it offers opportunities to make education more inclusive (offering text-to-speech and speech-to-text tools), progressive (providing feedback to students by giving immediate responses or identifying areas where they need more support) and personalized (by adapting to a student's pace and learning style and providing targeted instruction and practice at just the right time).
Outside The Classroom
It's not just inside the classroom where AI can help. Lesson preparation and administrative processes can be expedited, especially where statistics need to be analyzed or organized. With clear policies governing its use in schools, AI could also help with staff recruitment and retention. Prospective employees will appreciate knowing that AI applications are approved tools they can use to manage their workload efficiently.
6 Considerations For An AI Strategy
According to UNESCO, as of June 2023, less than 10% of schools and universities had implemented AI strategies or policies or set out guidance for its use in their institutions. If you haven’t done this already, now is the time! For all the positive things that AI is bringing to education, there are still risks. It can still make mistakes and make things up (hallucinate) and with so much staff, student and parent personally identifiable information (PII) held in schools and districts, guiding staff against entering any of it into generative AI tools is critical.
Collating all the knowledge you have gained from the experimentation period of the last 18 months to create purposeful guidelines for your school or district will help ensure everyone uses it ethically and in line with the standards you define. Consider these six points as you establish your AI strategy.
1. Vision
A good starting point is the advice set out by the World Economic Forum:
"AI should be employed purposefully to support and enrich the learning experience, promoting student and staff well-being, and enhancing administrative functions. The focus should be on using AI to help all students achieve educational goals while considering equity, inclusivity, and reducing the digital divide."
Sit down and discuss what you want AI to do. Don’t try to apply it to everything at once. Instead, take it step by step. Be selective and ensure that what you do with it works, then move on to the next phase.
2. Ethics
AI is still an ethical minefield, so raising awareness of that fact amongst the staff in your school is the mission here. Ensure that everyone knows that it learns from what we feed into it, and it’s for that reason that we should not place personal data anywhere near it.
Also, be sure to consult any local official guidance on AI’s use in education. This varies from location to location, and many countries and regions are still scrambling to keep up with its rapid pace of development.
3. Inclusion
Improving inclusion is critical. Using AI-based solutions such as real-time live captioning or audio description opens up access to information, enabling all students to access the same learning path at the same time. AI can also recognize speech and help students navigate websites by voice commands; provide an adaptive learning environment by adjusting the difficulty level of activities to move at the student’s pace; and analyze their data to spot any areas of challenge and enable early intervention to ensure understanding.
4. Parents
There is still much apprehension about the use of AI in schools, with some parents and guardians thinking that students will only use it to do their homework for them. So, it’s a good idea to inform them how your school plans to use AI tools constructively and give them a chance to ask questions, especially if educators will direct students to use these tools at home. Getting parents and guardians on board with your plans is not only courteous but also reassures them that they are considered and robust.
5. Training
As with any new technology tool, training is vital, and ongoing professional development is a must! Prompt crafting is an essential skill for educators to learn, so dedicate time for staff training and practice to enable them to maximize the technology.
AI is evolving rapidly, so keeping up with its capabilities (and risks) is vital, as is ensuring all staff are knowledgeable about any legislation or guidance published concerning its use in education.
6. Impact
Plan your objectives carefully and record the conditions before and after you test your AI tools. For example, if you want to see how AI can help educators with content curation, consider all the factors you will measure; it’s not exclusively about saving time. It’s also about ensuring quality and accuracy, keeping a check on bias and hallucination, and whether staff possess the necessary prompt crafting skills to produce relevant resources that sit in line with your curriculum.
Moving Forward
Whatever route your school takes, generative AI will certainly become a fixture of education in the future. However, remember that AI use is not the objective but is simply a tool to help achieve educational goals. Balance and human validation are key.

title: Council Post: How New LLM And LGM Technologies Can Improve Safety In The Fleet Transportation Industry
text:
David Julian is the CTO and cofounder of Netradyne.
No matter how adept a commercial driver is, factors out of their control can still lead to dangerous—and sometimes fatal—crashes. The statistics are alarming. According to the National Safety Council, in 2022, 5,837 trucks were involved in fatal crashes. That’s a 1.8% rise from 2021 and a 49% rise over the last decade. The NSC defines large trucks as “any medium or heavy truck, not including buses and motor homes, with a gross vehicle weight rating greater than 10,000 pounds.” This includes both commercial and non-commercial vehicles.
Every day, countless commercial vehicles, such as school buses and box trucks carrying goods, get on the road. The better commercial drivers are able to predict potential obstacles, the better they can navigate them and avoid collisions that could lead to the destruction of life, property or both. That’s where emerging large language model (LLM) and, more broadly, large generative model (LGM) technology can step in.
Baseline AI Is A Good Start For Driver Safety—But Has Limited Capabilities
Artificial intelligence isn’t new to the fleet transportation industry. Forward collision warning (FCW) and pedestrian collision warning (PCW) systems use AI—in general, a base layer of AI with heuristics running on top of it. These tools use radar or vision-based AI to essentially detect objects in front of drivers. They are capable of providing basic guidance to drivers in real time, alerting drivers that a pedestrian or animal has suddenly appeared in front of them, and using the relative speed of the vehicle and object to determine that if something about the situation doesn’t change in, say, two seconds, then there will be a collision.
But by nature, these tools aren’t anticipatory of many critical potential collision events. They can’t predict the complex cues that could lead to accidents, such as a pedestrian who is about to cross the street or a car that is about to merge in front of a driver. They can only pick up on what’s “in front of them,” so to speak.
New LLM And LGM Technologies Can Pick Up On Subtle Cues For Drivers
By contrast, more advanced LLM and LGM technologies (full disclosure: my company is working on one such solution that uses both) are capable of picking up on the subtle details of drivers’ surroundings and alerting them of situations where they need to take action.
ChatGPT has been trained on an enormous amount of data to understand human writing and speech patterns and predict the next sequence of words when prompted. Similarly, LLM and LGM technologies can be trained on a large amount of driving data, such as driving rules, subtle pedestrian and vehicle interactions and video clips of accidents around the world, to get to a point where it can predict the next frames of data—and make strong generalized collision warnings and recommendations. For example, new LLM and LGM technologies trained on hundreds of thousands of videos of pedestrian-vehicle collisions could learn that certain subtle cues indicate that a pedestrian is about to walk onto the road and give the driver a directive to slow down or stop.
Additionally, this technology can be used to give drivers more nuanced coaching, helping them become more adept at instinctively navigating potential hazards on the road. For instance, if a driver is bad at picking up cues from other vehicles that want to merge, the technology can guide them to become better at doing so. Or, the technology can be used in a simulated environment to show drivers the outcomes that could result from them taking different actions. This technology can also be used to reward good driver behavior, essentially gamifying safe driving.
However, as with any form of artificial intelligence, accuracy is key. Before these tools can be used on a day-to-day basis, they need to alert the driver with a low miss detect rate for impending collisions. But there’s a balance. The goal of achieving a low miss detect rate shouldn’t lead to overcorrection that generates too many false alarms or hallucinations from the models. Too many instances of “boy who cried wolf,” and drivers will stop paying attention to the predictions. The algorithms and KPIs must help drivers understand what’s in front of them, what’s highly likely to happen, what they’re doing right and wrong and what they should do.
The Path Forward
I predict this technology will first make headway in the commercial vehicle space, and will then eventually be used in personal vehicles as well. However, before this technology becomes widespread for either commercial or personal vehicles, it will need to be trained on large, vast data sets that cover different weather conditions, road types, vehicle categories and so forth.
But once these LLMs and LGMs have been sufficiently trained, they stand to increase ROI for companies that have fleets and improve driver training. And ultimately, and most importantly, new LLM and LGM technologies can make our roads safer, substantially reducing collisions—and saving lives.

title: For College Students—And For Higher Ed Itself—AI Is A Required Course
text:
Some of the nation’s biggest tech companies have announced efforts to reskill people to avoid job losses caused by artificial intelligence, even as they work to perfect the technology that could eliminate millions of those jobs.
It’s fair to ask, however: What should college students and prospective students, weighing their choices and possible time and financial expenses, think of this?
The news this spring was encouraging for people seeking to reinvent their careers—“reskilling”—to grab middle-class jobs and a shot at economic security.
“Tech giants hatch a plan for AI job losses: Reskill 95 million in 10 years,” reads one recent headline. The story details plans for a group including Google, IBM, Intel, and Microsoft to help people who have lost or are about to lose their jobs.
There are two sides to this: Learning about AI and other tech, and learning with those technologies. Online learning opportunities abound, as anyone knows who has turned to YouTube for instructions in cooking, car repairs, coding or a hundred other pursuits.
The big names are also pitching in to help learners understand the exploding field of artificial intelligence. For example, on its SkillsBuild learning portal, IBM offers a free credential in AI basics in a 10-hour online training program called AI Fundamentals.
Amazon, meanwhile, created the Generative AI Foundations series, which tech writer David Gewirtz calls an “all-you-can-eat buffet of really cool and really interesting material to learn and watch.”
While nobody knows how many jobs will be lost—or created—due to artificial intelligence, it’s already clear that AI, besides being a great subject for learning, will make it cheaper and more convenient to upskill and prepare for the future. AI will also be ubiquitous. Most major computer applications now have an “AI assistant.” Understanding how to use those and interpret what they share will help leverage human ability in our interaction with machines.
MIT Economics Professor David Autor is optimistic, writing that we should not be worried about having enough jobs.
“We are not running out of jobs. And, in fact, you know, all the Western world right now is in full or over-employment. And even during the whole computer revolution zone, we didn’t run out of jobs. It’s not the quantity that matters.”
Autor, co-director of the Labor Studies Program at the National Bureau of Economic Research, said in an interview with us that AI can help leverage expertise so workers can do higher-value work.
“I’m not Pollyanna about it. There will be real dislocation and displacement,” he said. “But there’s more upside and potential than with previous technology. AI will reshape the value and nature of human expertise. Expertise commands a market premium if it is both necessary for accomplishing an objective and relatively scarce.”
Tutoring is one promising area for AI, as is interactive learning through simulations of work environments. For example, pilots have long benefitted from training on simulators, and now AI is augmenting simulators for other skills in virtual reality platforms. One notable example: an AI-powered laparoscopic simulator to train surgeons to work inside the body using tools inserted through small incisions. In their training, the students get immediate feedback from the artificial intelligence system, which itself has been trained on the movements of experts.
Where does higher education fit into this? Many of those seeking to grow their skills online could be forgiven if they feel ill-served—left on their own to navigate the options and competing benefits of online learning. Yes, there’s an abundance of free online training—just as there’s always been an abundance of knowledge in libraries. But learning requires more than mere access to information—and higher ed can fill that gap. It has a natural role in presenting, explaining, and documenting learning—not just curating online resources. It adds value through quality instruction, broad-based learning, and partnerships with employers. Ideally, online learning tools will increasingly be embedded in longer learning paths that, should the learner wish, lead to college degrees.
Today’s colleges and universities face immense challenges, to be sure—but AI also presents them with a dual opportunity: They can use AI systems to educate people for good jobs more quickly and at less expense; and they can build instruction about AI itself across majors and disciplines.
Frankly, given AI’s inexorable progress, this is a path they must take. The rocketing pace of change demands that schools experiment, adapt, and collaborate as never before.
We may also need to adjust our advice for students of all ages and levels. The new message? Skill up—and keep it up. In today’s world, frequent reskilling is the only way to stay ahead of the game.

title: King's Speech Lays Out U.K.'s Plans For Tech Regulation
text:
Today's King's Speech has set out the new Labour government's plans for AI and cyber security, which have been broadly welcomed by the tech industry.
While falling short of promising an AI bill any time soon, the speech said that the government would "seek to establish the appropriate legislation to place requirements on those working to develop the most powerful artificial intelligence models".
The Labour party previously pledged to introduce binding regulation on those AI firms building the most powerful models—and it still remains to be seen what that legislation might entail.
"We look forward to seeing more detail about what the government means when it comes to placing appropriate requirements on those working to develop the most powerful artificial intelligence models. Most IT experts' concerns are not that AI is too powerful but that basic guardrails are not in place," comments Adam Leon Smith, of BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT.
"There must be high professional standards to ensure AI is directed and developed by individuals who adhere to agreed measures of competence and ethics. We advise against focusing too narrowly on a handful of companies."
Michal Szymczak, head of AI strategy at software consulting firm Zartis echoes these concerns, saying the government must avoid being too heavy-handed.
"I worry that any such policies could smother AI innovation in the crib with red tape, especially when factoring in any imposed costs of compliance. For startups especially, this could become a demoralizing deterrent," he says.
"The Labour manifesto clearly wants to strike a balance between nurturing innovation and regulating companies that are developing the most powerful AI models. It’s a nice sentiment in theory, but you can’t have your cake and eat it, too."
While any AI bill remains up in the air, two bills were announced in the speech: the Digital Information and Smart Data Bill and the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill.
The Digital Information and Smart Data Bill is aimed at encouraging the innovative use of data to help boost the economy. This would include the creation of new digital verification services, along with systems allowing customer data to be shared with authorized third-party service providers.
The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, meanwhile, is aimed at securing critical national infrastructure—particularly important given the recent attack on an NHS supplier, Synnovis, which resulted in the postponement of thousands of appointments and elective procedures. However, some industry observers—as you might expect—say they're concerned about over-regulation.
"It will be vital that the government work with industry to ensure that security requirements in the legislation are fit for purpose and strike the right balance between building resilience and fostering innovation," says Carla Baker, senior director for government affairs, UK & Ireland, at Palo Alto Networks.
"If we are to achieve sustained economic growth in the UK, organizations cannot be burdened with overly prescriptive requirements. The government must take a coordinated approach to developing policy interventions that protect critical sectors of society and drive economic growth, and refrain from producing guidance with overlapping or conflicting requirements."
The bill marks the first change to U.K. cybersecurity legislation in six years.
"Imagine how far behind we’ve fallen compared to the rapidly evolving capabilities of hostile actors in that time," says Al Lakhani, CEO of security firm IDEE.
"We can and must go further, and additional legislation and resources will be needed to tackle the ongoing risks facing the UK’s long-neglected digital infrastructure."

title: What We Can Learn From The First AI eSports Champion
text:
This year’s National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) Show offered the world a new form of entertainment that even Las Vegas hadn’t seen before: the world’s first creative AI eSports Tournament.
The tournament asked 16 contestants to use Leonardo.ai and its “Realtime Canvas” tool over 3 rounds. The contestants were judged for speed, accuracy and—as the winner later put it—“the least amount of weird AI hallucinations that can occur with generative AI.” But there are key takeaways here beyond the rules of the game. Namely that prompts aren’t everything and there’s an entertainment play to be made with AI.
Prompts Are Just The Beginning
With the rise in popularity of AI, prompts have become very important very quickly. An AI Prompt is any form of text, question, information, or coding that communicates to AI the type of response the user is seeking. Adjustments in the phrasing of an AI prompt have been shown to lead to varying responses. It is therefore unsurprising that prompt writing was a skill measured by this competition.
In one round, contestants were given a vague prompt (e.g., create a punk paradise) and then tasked with writing a prompt for Leonardo themselves. “For this one I created ‘a rocker teen with a blue mohawk playing guitar on the beach in Hawaii,” says tournament champion Jagger Waters, recounting a prompt she wrote.
However, prompt writing was was just the beginning. There were other skills that contestants had to demonstrate as well. One was using Leonardo’s “Realtime Canvas” tool to create a stick-figure drawing along with prompting the AI. As Waters describes it, “The realtime canvas lets you make a very rudimentary stick figure drawing of what you want to see, and it instantly creates a very high-resolution version of your idea. So you can create a prompt to get started, but get it even closer to what you're hoping for by using that tool. It helps you jump from ideation to execution.”
AI is Entertainment
AI is a tool, but this tournament also puts it forth as entertainment, and calling it eSports raises the question: is it really a game? YouTube content creator Devin Ricker, who was in attendance, reports that, “The tournament was really cool and surprisingly immersive like a close football game coming down to the wire.” And Fred Grinstein, also in attendance, says, “The event felt like Extreme Pictionary on a stage.”
In addition to being a game, the tournament itself was also a show. “The ‘performance’ aspect is why I think I succeeded,” says Waters, “I played to the audience. I was expressive and reactive. I made eye contact with them. The thrill of live performance is what made this compelling from a player POV: hearing the audience react in real-time to the smallest changes I made, hearing them cheer.” Audience response was also part of the event’s game-like nature: when the Judges votes were tied, the volume of audience cheers determined the winner.
Humans Are Essential
The competitors in this AI eSports tournament are skilled at using AI and a close viewing of their approaches and choices could certainly yield lessons for the spectator on a micro level, for example, how people can better work with AI on individual tasks. That being said, the tournament as a whole teaches us some lessons on a macro level. To use AI well will require more than just skill at prompt-writing and the structured use of AI can provide multiple types of entertainment media. These lessons show that while AI continues to become more prevalent in different industries, we consistently see that the growth of AI continues to emphasize unique contributions that humans make.

title: Council Post: Energy Management: The Use Of Wasted Energy For AI Computing
text:
Adrien Nejkovic is CEO at Hearst Capital: Pioneering sustainable tech & finance with AI, blockchain and renewable energy.
As the world becomes increasingly digital, the demand for computing power has skyrocketed. Technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain have emerged as transformative forces but also have significant energy requirements. As an entrepreneur deeply involved in the tech industry, I have had the unique opportunity to negotiate and implement the use of wasted energy for AI computing and blockchain mining. This experience has not only opened my eyes to the immense potential of this approach but has also convinced me that it represents the future of energy management.
The Challenge Of Energy Consumption
AI computing and blockchain mining are notoriously energy-intensive processes. AI algorithms require substantial computational power to train and operate, while blockchain mining involves solving complex mathematical problems, necessitating vast amounts of electricity. Traditionally, this has led to significant environmental concerns, with critics pointing out the substantial carbon footprint associated with these technologies.
However, the growing emphasis on sustainability has spurred the search for more efficient and eco-friendly energy solutions. This is where the concept of utilizing wasted energy comes into play. Wasted energy refers to the excess energy produced by industrial processes or renewable energy sources that would otherwise go unused. By redirecting this energy towards AI computing and blockchain mining, we can significantly reduce the environmental impact of these technologies.
My Journey Into Wasted Energy Utilization
My journey into this innovative approach began while exploring ways to optimize energy use in our AI-driven projects. I realized that a significant amount of energy generated by various industrial processes was being wasted, so I investigated how we could harness this excess energy for our computational needs.
The first step was to identify potential sources of wasted energy. We focused on industries known for high energy consumption and significant waste, such as manufacturing and power generation. Partnering with these industries required extensive negotiations. We needed to demonstrate the mutual benefits of redirecting their wasted energy to our operations. This involved detailed presentations on how this approach could enhance their sustainability efforts, improve their corporate social responsibility profiles and potentially offer financial incentives through energy credits or reduced operational costs.
The Negotiation Process
Negotiating these partnerships was no small feat. It required a deep understanding of both the industrial and technological landscapes. One key challenge was convincing industry stakeholders of the feasibility and reliability of using their wasted energy for our purposes. Many were initially skeptical and concerned about the stability of the energy supply and the technical challenges in transferring energy from their processes to our computing facilities.
To address these concerns, we conducted pilot projects demonstrating this approach and the benefits of practical applications. We partnered with several manufacturing plants that produced significant waste heat. By installing heat recovery systems, we will convert this heat into electricity, which will then be used to power our AI data centers. The success of this study provided a compelling proof of concept, which helped gain the trust and cooperation of other industry partners.
The Benefits Of Wasted Energy Utilization
The benefits of utilizing wasted energy for AI computing and blockchain mining are manifold. Firstly, it significantly reduces the carbon footprint associated with these technologies. By tapping into energy that would otherwise go unused, we minimize the demand for additional power generation, which often relies on fossil fuels.
Secondly, this approach enhances the overall efficiency of energy use. Industrial processes become more sustainable as their energy waste is repurposed productively. This not only supports environmental goals but also offers economic benefits. Industries can lower their energy costs and earn incentives for contributing to sustainable energy practices.
Moreover, using wasted energy can lead to more resilient and decentralized energy systems. Instead of relying solely on traditional power grids, which can be vulnerable to disruptions, AI and blockchain operations can benefit from multiple, diverse energy sources. This diversification enhances the stability and reliability of the energy supply for these critical technologies.
The Future Of Energy Management
The successful integration of wasted energy utilization into AI computing and blockchain mining represents a significant step forward in energy management. As the demand for computational power continues to grow, finding sustainable energy solutions becomes imperative. My experience has shown that we can turn potential environmental liabilities into assets with the right approach and partnerships.
Looking ahead, I believe this model can be scaled and applied globally. Governments and regulatory bodies can play a crucial role by creating policies and incentives that encourage wasted energy use. For instance, offering tax breaks or subsidies for companies that implement energy recovery systems can accelerate the adoption of this practice.
Furthermore, technological advancements will continue to improve the efficiency and feasibility of energy recovery and utilization. Innovations in energy storage, grid integration and heat recovery systems will enhance our ability to effectively capture and repurpose wasted energy.
Conclusion
My journey into negotiating the use of wasted energy for AI computing and blockchain mining has been enlightening and rewarding. This approach not only addresses the energy challenges associated with these technologies but also paves the way for more sustainable and efficient energy management practices. By harnessing wasted energy, we can support the growth of AI and blockchain in an environmentally responsible manner, contributing to a more sustainable future.
As we move forward, it is essential for industry stakeholders, policymakers and technologists to collaborate and explore innovative solutions like this. The future of energy management lies in our ability to adapt and optimize our resources. Utilizing wasted energy is a powerful example of how we can turn challenges into opportunities, ensuring our technological advancements align with our environmental responsibilities.

title: Council Post: How Generative AI Can Improve Employee Productivity And Happiness
text:
Andrey Kalyuzhnyy, CEO of 8allocate. As a technology leader, Andrey helps businesses overcome challenges with tailored software solutions.
Since ChatGPT's public launch, opinions on generative AI have split. On one side, there are fears of job displacement, redundancies and layoffs. On the other side, there is an almost futuristic belief in human-machine synergy, ushering in a new era of economic prosperity.
Generative AI (GenAI) won’t replace humans or enable fully autonomous operations in the foreseeable future. What these technologies can offer now and in the future is immersive skills augmentation, making the workforce smarter, more effective and more satisfied.
Understanding Generative AI
Generative AI models produce text, visual and audio inputs based on the training data. Because they’re trained on a large corpus of public knowledge, their outputs reflect common human behaviors, practices and ways of thinking.
This makes Generative AI a helpful assistant for a variety of tasks—programming, data modeling, text summarization and media materials creation—but not an independent executioner. GenAI tools are great at “co-piloting”—assisting the workforce with routine, repetitive and time-consuming tasks.
The Positive Impacts Of Generative AI
As a technology leader and AI enthusiast, I’ve been involved with custom AI solutions development and the fine-tuning of open-source LLMs. My conclusion is that generative AI will bring the strongest impact on workforce productivity and creativity. Here are a few examples:
Higher Productivity
The flip side of digital transformation is growing data silos. An average enterprise now uses 1,061 different applications, with only 29% being integrated. Lack of integration forces workers to switch screens, do manual data entry and spend time hunting down relevant information. This prolongs onboarding for new hires, increases information asymmetry and breeds operational inefficiencies.
GenAI can improve knowledge management. Thanks to retrieval augmented generation (RAG), open-source LLMs can be fine-tuned to search connected databases, identify relevant information and produce a contextually relevant response. Thomson Reuters, for example, created an AI assistant that produces relevant answers based on expertise contributed by legal subject matter experts and attorney editors.
Generative AI tools bring in a conversational interface for data analysis. Instead of complex technical queries, users can use text commands to access and analyze data across multiple dimensions. Colgate-Palmolive created a GenAI tool to synthesize consumer and shopper insights, understand consumer sentiment and inform product development. Enterra Solutions, likewise, built a System of Intelligence platform that supplies advanced consumer intelligence, growth insights, demand and supply analytics and competitor analysis to enterprises. (Disclosure: Enterra is one of 8allocate's partners.)
Enhanced Creativity
GenAI models also bring a new degree of efficiency to the creation processes. An Adobe survey found that 66% of creative professionals use AI to improve content and 58% use it to increase content production volumes.
In EdTech, generative AI tools are proving useful in curriculum development and content authoring. Fine-tuned LLMs can generate instructional materials from corporate documents and policies. Likewise, they can help trainers produce personalized materials for different learner cohorts. Amira Learning, for instance, built an adaptive tutoring system for improving reading skills. Similar solutions are also coming to the corporate training market.
GenAI also reduces the cost and complexities of creating immersive simulation training in AR or VR formats. With GenAI tools, companies can create realistic training scenarios for soft and hard skills. AR and VR also improve product development processes, allowing teams to virtually iterate on complex concepts before creating physical prototypes.
Lastly, data and creativity are mutually reinforcing—and GenAI tools commoditized access to advanced forecasting. Some of the best ideas are born at the intersection of seemingly unrelated industries or creative takes on existing solutions.
Understanding Your Readiness For GenAI Adoption
GenAI adoption requires organizational readiness in terms of people, processes and technology. Organizations risk facing spiraling costs, compliance issues and low ROI without proper preparations.
To unlock the full potential of GenAI, evaluate your maturity in these four areas:
• Strategy And Governance: Can you identify and objectively evaluate promising GenAI use cases in your business? Work backward from your goals (e.g., cost optimization or productivity gains) to narrow down your focus. Determine which KPIs can be a good proxy for measuring the impact. Model expected usage patterns and solution cost to better estimate the ROI for selected use cases and secure executive-level sponsorship.
• Data Organization: Even off-the-shelf GenAI tools require a strong technical baseline of cloud computing and mature data management practices. Data silos, system interoperability issues and a lack of unified data governance strategies undermine your ability to quickly iterate on different GenAI use cases. You may need to implement changes to your data pipelines to improve data integration across systems and implement proper controls for ensuring data privacy, security and ethical usage.
• Technology Competence: GenAI model fine-tuning and implementation requires a somewhat different skill set than traditional software engineering and data science. Do you have the qualified talent to advise you on the technical feasibility of selected use cases and set up an effective model development process? Perhaps you may need a new role(s) to lead and execute GenAI-related initiatives.
• Skills And Culture: GenAI adoption may be met with skepticism by employees who are unfamiliar with it. Over 67% of senior managers don’t feel comfortable using advanced AI and data analytics tools. How are you planning to educate your people on the benefits, risks and limitations of new tools? Your workforce must understand the appropriate usage scenarios and governance steps, as well as feel empowered to use the technology available to them.
Mature organizations develop internal AI governance frameworks to ensure safe technology adoption and effective change management. A typical framework covers privacy, ethics, compliance, performance, operations and security controls in place for the adopted systems.
In conclusion, generative AI technologies can improve operating efficiencies, workforce productivity and employee satisfaction from the work they get to do. However, GenAI adoption also requires prudence from the executive teams, especially amid emerging AI regulations like the National Privacy Bill and the EU AI Act.
Start having an open dialog at every level about the benefits and risks GenAI can bring into your organization to identify the optimal use cases, address skepticism and create excitement about the technology’s vast potential.
