title: ‘Human Intelligence’ Art Movement Takes Defiant Stand Against AI
text:
Procrastinating on her work as a book illustrator one day, Beth Spencer picked up an iPad and sketched a red hand jotting the words “created with human intelligence.” She’d seen a lot of concerned chatter about AI among fellow artists on Instagram, and she figured she’d post the drawing to her website to emphasize that everything visitors see there originates with a blood-and-bone artist.
In a Substack post, Spencer gave other artists permission to add the badge to their own sites for free—as long as they did so to spotlight work made without help from artificial intelligence. “I thought maybe two or three people would say, ‘Thanks, I’ll take one,’ because people love free stuff, right?” Spencer said. Instead, around 50 artists and writers requested the image below on the first day.
Sensing she’d hit a collective nerve, Spencer then posted her image to Instagram and invited other artists to draw it in their own style using any materials (save for AI, of course). Popular “Draw this in your style” challenges fill the social media platform, but this marked Spencer’s first time hosting one.
“It’s just exploded,” the artist said over the phone from her home in Memphis, Tennessee, where she’s illustrating a children’s picture book, due out in March. “It’s been really exciting to see all the creativity that could come from a scrappy little five-minute sketch that I made when I was supposed to be doing work.”
Since Spencer first announced the challenge in early June, nearly 1,200 artists, illustrators and designers have contributed their own versions of her drawing to a growing gallery of unique images that all underscore the same defiant message: Amid the proliferation of art by algorithms, human artists cannot, and should not, be replaced. (Click on the images in this article to learn more about the artists.)
“It’s not saying AI should be banned,” Spencer clarified of the initiative. “It’s more pro-human than anti-tech.”
Submissions to the human intelligence challenge have flooded in from the U.S., U.K, Spain, Germany, Italy, Brazil and beyond as generative AI continues to provoke passionate responses from artists across genres. Some hail it as a promising new tool that can steer them in surprising and wonderful directions. Others worry companies are stealing their work to train AI datasets without credit or compensation. They fear AI will take their jobs, and possibly alter the very nature of creativity.
The project gets to complex questions at the heart of the debate over AI and art. Can art made with artificial intelligence convey the raw human emotion and passion of a lived experience? Creatives have conflicting opinions, but not surprisingly, the artists participating in Spencer’s challenge fall in the skeptical camp.
“My work has always been created by hand, and there is no way to replicate the feelings it provokes through those hand-drawn lines and layers,” Brooklyn-based artist, author and teacher Samantha Dion Baker wrote when posting her badge to Instagram.
Artists like Baker increasingly are relying on the conduit they know best, their art, to counter the rushing AI tide. Last month, a photographer who won an AI photo contest got disqualified after he revealed he’d submitted a real photo to prove that human-generated art hasn’t lost its impact in a world of algorithms.
Christopher Thornock, a freelance illustrator and gallery artist in Utah and a professor of illustration at Utah Valley University, said he doesn’t usually participate in “Draw this in your style” challenges. This one felt different.
“I have concerns over what might come from the use of AI imagery in my industry,” he said. “It felt like a way to show solidarity with other artists and illustrators.”
His contribution looks like it’s composed with graphite, but he made it on an iPad with the program Procreate and custom digital brushes. Many contributors to the human intelligence challenge also went the digital route for their badges. Others opted for ink, pastels, colored pencils, watercolor paint, paper collage or claymation.
Mateo Montoya’s whimsical take features a hand that looks like it belongs to a character from Nick Park, creator of “Wallace & Gromit” and “Shaun the Sheep.” The hand holds a red pencil as it completes a circle around “created with human intelligence,” the words that appear in Spencer’s original sketch.
The Colombian artist sculpted the hand out of the crafting material known as cold porcelain, then covered it with acrylic paint and dressed it in shirt and jacket sleeves he fashioned from fabric. He spent about two days on the project.
“What we illustrators, designers and artists do not only fulfills an aesthetic function, it fulfills a communicative function,” Montoya said over email. “Our work is a very powerful tool to express what we think and feel.”
Spencer echoes that sentiment, though she doesn’t identify as firmly anti-AI can’t say artificial intelligence will never make its way into her artwork. AI-generated images as they currently stand, however, don’t impress her.
“They all kind of look greasy to me, like they’ve been dipped in oil,” she said. “People will get tired of seeing shiny images.”
The human intelligence art challenge continues through the end of August, at which point Spencer plans to randomly select a winner from all entrants. That person will win a complimentary $70 annual membership to the Introvert Drawing Club, an online art community founded by Spencer that offers drawing sessions and whose 7,000 members share art prompts, tips and techniques.
It’s clearly not the prize that’s motivating artists to showcase the hands of humans in making art, however.
“I hope that our viewers see we want to connect through the works of our hands, heads and hearts,” Thornock said. “That there is experience and soul behind what we do.”

title: ASML Stock Up 49% In 2024, Falls On Fear Of China Export Curbs
text:
Demand for machines used to build computer chips is likely to increase due to the boom in demand for generative artificial intelligence.
One company, Netherlands-based ASML, is the world’s dominant supplier of these extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines — which “are required to manufacture the most advanced chips,” noted CNBC.
ASML’s machines are expensive and take a long time to build. “Sporting a price tag of over $300 million each, in November 2023, buyers faced a two-year wait once they placed an order,” noted my new book, Brain Rush.
ASML’s second quarter 2024 results beat expectations due to demand for AI chips. Nevertheless, ASML shares fell 9% on fear of a decline in demand for its machines in China as a result of more export curbs, reported Barron’s.
The drop in ASML shares could represent a buying opportunity as demand for the company’s product rises in in 2025 and beyond.
ASML’s Second Quarter 2024 Results
ASML’s stock had risen 49% in 2024 as of July 16, yet the company’s shares fell after reporting expectations-beating results.
Here are the key numbers:
- Q2 2024 net sales: $6.8 billion — down 9.5% but $1.3 billion ahead of expectations, according to the London Stock Exchange Group.
- Q2 2024 net profit: $1 45 billion — down 18.7% but $130 million more than expected, noted LSEG.
- Q2 2024 net bookings: $5.2 billion — 24% more than the previous year, CNBC reported.
- Q3 2024 net sales forecast: $6.44 billion at the range midpoint — $550 million below analysts’ expectations, according to CNBC.
ASML expressed optimism about the company’s future. “We currently see strong developments in AI, driving most of the industry recovery and growth, ahead of other market segments,” ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet said in a statement.
Nevertheless, worries about the future persist. “While there are still uncertainties in the market, primarily driven by the macro environment, we expect industry recovery to continue in the second half of the year,” Fouquet said.
“We see 2024 as a transition year with continued investments in both capacity ramp and technology. We currently see strong developments in AI, driving most of the industry recovery and growth, ahead of other market segments,” he added.
“EUV orders increased substantially” in the quarter, Mihuzo Securities analyst Kevin Wang told Reuters. “We attribute this to strong orders from TSMC and Intel.”
ASML has been under government pressure — from the U.S. and the Netherlands — to restrict exports of its latest EUV machines to China.
The company said such restrictions would “impact 10% to 15% of it’s China sales this year,” CNBC reported. In the second quarter of 2024, 49% of ASML’s business came from exporting its older equipment to China, according to Reuters.
Prospects For ASML’s Stock Price
ASML stock is slightly under-valued according to Wall Street analysts. Based on three analysts offering 12-month price targets for ASML Holding the stock would need to rise 2.3% to reach the average of $1,092.50, noted TipRanks.
Demand for EUVs could pick up in 2025 — thus resulting in faster than anticipated growth in ASML revenues.
Last year, Jeffries forecast strong demand from TSMC driven by growth in AI.
Specifically, TSMC was anticipated to use ASML machines to build 5 nanometer and 3 nanometer parts “to power machine learning and AI training and inference workloads,” note Brain Rush. Jeffries estimated ASML’s revenue growth would average 21% between 2022 and 2025.
ASML confirmed such demand from TSMC and Samsung. “The industry expects to be in a cyclical upturn in 2025, Fouquet said in a pre-recorded video addressing the company’s Q2 2024 earnings, reported CNBC.
“As a result, we need to prepare for a number of new fabs that are being built today across the globe. Those fabs will be spread geographically and are strategic for all our customers. They are all scheduled to take our systems,” he added.
Another analyst expects AI to account for a growing share of ASML’s revenues. AI is a “relatively small part” of ASML revenues, Ben Barringer, Quilter Cheviot technology analyst, told CNBC. “But that’s going to grow very significantly over the next little while,” added Barringer.
Will The U.S. Protect Taiwan?
The upcoming presidential election could make things more difficult for ASML.
If Biden wins a second term, export restrictions on ASML could increase. “The Biden administration is said to be considering implementing more restrictions on ASML Holding that would prevent it from selling equipment to China,” notes Bloomberg.
If former president Donald Trump wins, Taiwan may not receive U.S. military protection from an invasion by China, “I think, Taiwan should pay us for defense,” Trump said in an interview with Bloomberg Businessweek. “You know, we’re no different than an insurance company. Taiwan doesn’t give us anything,” he added.
Whether a killer app emerges for generative AI is likely to be more important for ASML’s future than the U.S. election results.
That’s because demand for GPUs will flatten — along with the urge to buy ASML’s machines — unless companies find a way to make their investments in generative AI pay off.

title: AI Adoption Is Driving Real Top - And Bottom-Line Impact For Enterprises
text:
The past year has witnessed the swift adoption of generative AI (genAI), and companies are beginning to see the results. According to Forrester’s Q2 AI Pulse Survey, 2024, consisting of generative AI decision-maker respondents, the top three positive impacts that companies report as a result of adopting genAI are improved customer experience (42%), increased employee productivity (40%), and increased revenues (34%). Enterprises with genAI FOMO should:
- Get familiar with generative AI terminology. Large language models are just one component of the generative AI ecosystem. A new vocabulary is emerging to describe different models, prompting techniques, and customization approaches. Business leaders, data and tech leaders, and data professionals should familiarize themselves with these emerging terms to ensure that they’re all speaking the same language.
- Select the right use cases based on industry and business function. While generative AI is a technology with horizontal relevance, it is impacting different industry verticals in very different ways. Use cases in healthcare, for example, look very different than they do in insurance or banking, and HR use cases differ significantly from marketing ones. Prioritize the use cases that make sense in the context of your business and that align with your strategy.
- Adopt an “align by design” approach. A lack of trust, privacy and security concerns, and risk and governance issues are the greatest barriers companies face in adopting generative AI. For the past six months we have been researching AI alignment, and what we’ve found is concerning. Misalignment is inevitable, but a proactive approach can mitigate risk.
AI Is Also Benefiting The World At Large
It is not just enterprises and technology vendors reaping the rewards of AI. A host of companies, NGOs, and governments are also using AI to make a positive impact on people and the planet. Here are three areas where this is happening:
- Mental health treatment. Predictive AI has been used for years in medical diagnosis, and now generative AI is making its way into mental health treatment. Earlier this year, Cedars-Sinai launched its eXtended-Reality Artificially Intelligent Ally, a physician-developed chatbot offering conversational therapy in immersive virtual reality environments. And in India, Iwill Therapy is leveraging Microsoft to offer chatbot-based cognitive behavioral therapy via its app in a host of local languages.
- Digital accessibility. One of the promises of generative AI is the democratization of access to the digital realm. Earlier this year, Apple began autogenerating transcriptions to Apple podcasts, which both opened up access for podcast consumers who are deaf or hard of hearing and also helped people with certain cognitive disabilities, people who prefer to read (versus listening) to learn, and anyone who wants to be able to search an episode to find specific content of interest.
- Sustainability. Given all the talk about AI’s carbon footprint, it may seem disingenuous to talk about AI and sustainability in the same breath, but some companies are using AI to mitigate environmental impact. In agriculture, for example, farms are combining robotics and AI technology to reduce herbicide use by up to 90%. Studies have shown that smart sensors with AI can reduce water consumption by over 40%. And AI research collective, the Mila Institute, is leveraging generative AI to visualize the future impact of climate change at any specific address, anywhere in the world.
Remember that genAI is just a technology, and like all other technologies, it can be used for good or for ill and applied well or poorly.
This post was written by VP, Principal Analyst Brandon Purcell and it originally appeared here.

title: If Only AI Developers Could Manage Expectations Like A TV Screenwriter
text:
Before streaming and binge-watching took over, television aficionados had to patiently wait for their favorite shows to come on. (Example: In Back to the Future, George McFly initially won’t ask Lorraine to the Enchantment Under the Sea Dance because he will miss his favorite show.)
That was in 1955.
As far back as the 1990s, NBC’s Must-See TV featured hit sitcoms such as Cheers, Seinfeld, and Mad About You on Thursdays. Those were the days—and nights—when our favorite shows were an event—not just some series to be consumed in one sitting. Instead of having entire seasons (or full shows) drop in an instant, we breathlessly anticipated each episode’s return, building suspense while allowing us time to discuss plotlines with friends. Each week brought a new wave of excitement as families gathered around TV sets, remote in hand, ready for the latest twists and turns.
Back in those days, season after season, we’d speculate on character arcs and storylines, debating series’ finer points, especially unforgettable cliffhangers. Who remembers the palpable tension of waiting to see if Ross and Rachel would ever hook up on Friends? Or the collective gasp when Hank finally realized Walter White’s identity while on the toilet in Breaking Bad? Water cooler conversations the next day were packed with theories and heated exchanges, adding to the magic of the viewing experience.
Then there was Lost—six seasons of electrifying TV that had viewers on the edge of their seats, endlessly theorizing about the island's mysteries and its inhabitants’ fates. Despite the ending being a massive disappointment, the journey itself was mesmerizing. A decade later, Game of Thrones followed a similar path, capturing imaginations and dominating pop culture, only to falter in its final episodes. Yet, the thrill of watching those epic battles and intricate political maneuvers live was something special.
So, what do all these shows have in common?
They played with audiences’ expectations, in some cases resulting in satisfaction—in others—creating disappointment. Zooming out, any kind of writing—whether we’re talking about screenwriting or blogging—is a craft where you’re constantly managing audience's expectations. As a content creator, you must guide people down a certain path, weaving a narrative that follows or subverts assumptions. How you pull off that delicate dance of anticipation and revelation is the hallmark of a skilled storyteller.
Interestingly, today’s business leaders are learning to adopt these narrative techniques. Whether the finished product is an eBook or a white paper, the real trick is understanding your audience and skillfully directing their journey, making the experience compelling.
More importantly, it’s about delivering.
Speaking of managing expectations, AI is the latest “shiny object” in tech and investor speculation. Just check out NVIDIA’s latest stock price! Much like blockchain and crypto before it, AI is all the rage in boardrooms and in the zeitgeist, setting minds on fire with its transformative promise. Decades after the AI Winter doldrums, it’s bursting with real-world applications that are already reshaping industries, from healthcare to finance.
While AI's transformative potential is undeniable, not all advancements have been smooth sailing. A prime example is Rabbit r1. Marketed as a revolutionary personal assistant, it promised to handle a wide range of tasks, from managing schedules and sending reminders to controlling smart home devices and providing personalized recommendations.
However, the reality has been far less impressive. Marques Brownlee, top tech content creator and YouTuber reviewed the r1 to much disappointment. In an April video titled Barely Reviewable, Brownlee dissects its pitfalls. In a detailed analysis, Brownlee points out critical flaws that undermined the user experience.
One of Brownlee's main criticisms concerned r1's poor voice recognition capabilities. He showed multiple instances where the assistant failed to understand basic commands or misinterpreted them entirely.
Such inconsistency made it unreliable for even the simplest tasks, such as setting reminders or controlling smart home devices. It’s not like Brownlee is out to besmirch this company’s reputation either. His main concern is not just with Rabbit, but with the larger trend of tech companies rolling out half-baked AI products, only to add the real features in later versions.
Rabbit r1's struggles underscore the fact that despite the hype, not all AI innovations can deliver on expectations. They also remind us that while AI’s potential is massive, achieving reliable and effective solutions requires careful planning, extensive testing, and a commitment to quality.
This “2.0” kind of technique may work if the initial product has legs, but promises can’t substitute real functionality. When a product is released, it should have full capability. Just like how a show should deliver on its big entertainment promises. Yes, I am referring to Lost again. (I still haven’t gotten over that disappointing finale.)
Just like the cultural juggernaut that is the Internet, artificial intelligence will soon transform everything in life from work to leisure to creativity—and now even children’s toys? Yet like so many TV shows, newfangled AI products must live up to the hype—or users and investors will tune out.
Big talk is exciting and fun, but not if audiences’ expectations aren’t met. Memories of eagerly anticipating TV episodes, dissecting plot twists with friends, and debating cliffhangers highlight how vital it is to manage audience expectations, a skill crucial not only in storytelling but also in tech. Just like screenwriters and business leaders, tomorrow’s AI developers must nail the art of guiding the public toward a happy, satisfying ending.

title: The XR Industry Reminds Us That AI Is Nothing New At AWE 2024
text:
This year’s Augmented World Expo 2024 was held in a new location: Long Beach, California. At the event, Oculus founder Palmer Luckey reminded the audience that Long Beach is where some of the earliest prototypes of the Oculus Rift were born, so in a sense AWE has come full circle by moving south from Santa Clara. While the event had a few stumbles in the new venue, such as out-of-focus projectors, the show also had plenty of highlights, including recognizing a lineup of industry veterans as newly inducted members of the XR Hall of Fame.
All in all, the Long Beach Convention Center felt like a much more spacious and well-situated venue for a big show with over 6,500 attendees in its 15th year. This year’s conference showcased many companies giving updates about their existing platforms, while others introduced new products—many of which were accelerated by AI.
HaptX G1 Gloves Are Ready For The Market At Last
Before the show began, HaptX invited me to the company’s demo suite to try out the HaptX G1, the company’s commercially ready haptic gloves for VR. HaptX has been around for a long time, but this is the first time that the company has shown off a market-ready product that is no longer a prototype. The HaptX G1 gloves are clearly more robust and easier to put on than the earlier development kits and prototypes I’ve tried, plus they come with a fully self-contained backpack.
In previous years, the complete system (DK1 and DK2) was very clunky. Even when the company implemented the backpack in DK2, it still had to connect to another box, which impeded cable-free use. Now, with the HaptX G1, you can finally have cable-free VR experiences. As part of this, the backpack has gotten larger, but on the positive side it’s now a very buttoned-up experience.
These gloves are still the gold standard for haptics in VR, and one of the most interesting developments for HaptX is that they are now being used to generate training data used in AI models intended for robots. HaptX customers are using real human input from these gloves to train robotic AI models with hundreds of data points and much finer granularity than is available from video inputs. This application excites me for the future.
Qualcomm’s Strategic Partnerships And Alignment With Google
Qualcomm was the only platinum sponsor for the show this year and again had the opening keynote immediately following the typically unorthodox welcome keynote from Ori Inbar, AWE’s Founder. The company had many walk-ons including NTT DoCoMo’s Qonoq division, which showed off its new XR headset—the first to feature Qualcomm’s AR2 Gen 1 chipset—which I got to try out at Qualcomm’s booth. Qualcomm also had Sony on stage to talk about the Spatial Content Creation System, which I tried out (and wrote about) back in April. Qualcomm also had Meta on stage to talk about the two companies’ partnership and how Qualcomm is pivotal in enabling Meta’s new Horizon OS, which will drive third-party headsets from companies including Lenovo and ASUS.
Qualcomm also announced that its Spaces platform would be compatible with Google’s upcoming XR platform. This makes sense when you consider that Google and Samsung have already announced that they will use Qualcomm’s XR2+ Gen 2 for their upcoming headset running Google’s XR platform. This is especially important for developers building apps who want to ship now and not wait until Google’s XR platform launches later this year. This is a pretty significant strategic shift from Qualcomm and shows a much closer alignment between Google and Qualcomm, something that’s been sorely missing for years.
Qualcomm also appointed a new head of its XR division, Ziad Asghar, who replaced the long-serving Hugo Swart—who recently moved to Google as senior director of ecosystem strategy and technology. Asghar’s experience in Qualcomm’s AI division gives him valuable insight because of how much of XR today is driven by AI and how XR, in turn, is going to be one of the biggest drivers for AI applications. This is a significant change because Swart helped get Qualcomm to its market-dominant position and will now be at Google, which I believe will help to further align the two companies. Asghar’s experience in AI will absolutely drive Qualcomm’s XR strategy further towards AI use cases.
XREAL Beam Pro Launches Globally
I’ve known about XREAL’s Beam Pro, a handheld XR compute device, for months and thought it would be an AWE exclusive. The company instead decided to announce it in China a few weeks ahead of AWE. While I know that China is a huge market for the company, the announcement did take some of the excitement out of the Beam Pro at AWE 2024. That said, I do believe that the Beam Pro is the right solution for the AR market as it stands today because it runs the Google Play store and has ample capabilities that make it exciting for future AR applications. The Beam Pro will enable the use of Android applications, and I believe that XREAL will likely serve as one of Google’s key partners in relaunching its XR ecosystem. This means that most Android apps, including GeForce Now and Xbox xCloud gaming services, can easily be blown up into huge virtual screens.
The Beam Pro uses a Qualcomm Snapdragon chipset and a display to help users utilize their XREAL AR glasses without needing to drain their phone’s battery. I have a review unit of the XREAL Beam Pro in my hands, and I expect to write a detailed review once I’ve had a chance to put it through its paces.
The Beam Pro is an evolution of XREAL’s original Beam, which was designed to enable XREAL’s glasses to have multiple display modes and be compatible with more devices. Beyond that, it also served as a battery for the XREAL glasses. The Beam Pro takes things much further by adding significantly more processing capability, a 3-D camera and a screen. Some might think of this as a smartphone without cellular connectivity, but it is more of a tiny tablet. The Beam Pro comes in configurations with 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage or 8GB of RAM and 512GB of storage; these start at $199, but XREAL is offering a $50 rebate for anyone with an existing first-generation Beam.
Sightful’s Spacetop G1 Commercial Launch
The Spacetop G1 is Sightful’s commercially ready version of the Spacetop AR laptop that the company announced last year. The Spacetop G1 still leverages custom XREAL glasses for display and still utilizes Qualcomm’s QCS8550 chipset, which is like the Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 but designed for much broader applications. It is a little bit surprising that Sightful is no longer using an XR2 chip when you consider that this is an AR laptop and it will most likely run AR applications in the near future. That said, this chipset is an upgrade in terms of performance and should perform similarly to an XR2 Gen 2 chip.
When I saw the Spacetop G1 at AWE, I was quite impressed with the refinement of the design from a year ago. I especially like that the company still understands what users need, for instance by providing dual USB-C ports and using a decent 60Wh battery, which could bode well for battery life. One of the less-known features of the Spacetop G1 is that it supports Wi-Fi 7 and 5G via SIM card and eSIM, which makes it extremely portable and enables true mobile productivity. The Spacetop G1 also finally has a release date in October, with preorders now open at a price of $1,900. At that price point, this is still clearly very much a product for enterprises and business users first.
DigiLens ARGO Goes Nuclear And Gets Google Gemini
At AWE, DigiLens once again had a major presence with a multitude of announcements. Last year it announced a slew of partnerships, and the momentum isn’t stopping this year with even bigger ones. Building on last year’s partnership, industry software leader Taqtile announced that its Manifest Work Instruction Platform would be available for DigiLens’s ARGO smart glasses. This partnership also enables DigiLens to work with the U.S. Department of Defense’s Defense Logistics Agency to improve logistics. Meanwhile, ManoMotion announced a collaboration with DigiLens to support the ARGO glasses with its hand interaction technologies, further enhancing the AR experience for ARGO users while also giving ManoMotion a wider market outside VR.
An even bigger partnership was announced by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge Enhanced Technology and Training Center, which will work alongside DigiLens with Consolidated Nuclear Security, operator of the Y-12 National Security Complex at Oak Ridge. This partnership will enable ARGO to be used in a broad array of applications including nuclear material processing.
Last but certainly not least, DigiLens also announced a partnership with Google that makes ARGO the first standalone AR glasses to run Google’s latest Gemini LLM. I tried this out on the noisy and congested convention floor, asking it a simple image query about what I was looking at and was quite impressed with how well it worked under such challenging conditions. I am excited to see how much of the Gemini LLM the companies will be able to run on-device and how much of it will have to run on the cloud. Regardless, having the power of one of the world’s leading LLMs on a pair of AR smart glasses brings us closer to the happy marriage of XR and AI that I believe will be a net positive for both industries.
Ultraleap Hyperion, A Pivot That Possibly Comes Too Late
At AWE 2024, Ultraleap demonstrated its recently announced Hyperion platform. Hyperion is a big deal because OEMs had to incorporate Ultraleap’s hardware in their devices for the longest time to get Ultraleap’s world-class hand tracking. This complicated the overall design of devices and added more cost to the bill of materials, which of course OEMs hate to do. So naturally, Ultraleap’s deployments were fairly few and far between—but they were fantastic when you did get them. Now, thanks to Hyperion, devices can use standard RGB cameras with the same hand-tracking algorithms, which means that ODMs such as Goertek are able to offer Ultraleap’s hand-tracking capabilities without any additional hardware.
At the event, Hyperion was also demonstrated running on multiple different platforms. One prototype solution used an event-based motion-tracking sensor from Prophesee attached to Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses so the user could control their music solely through gestures. This would be an extremely low-power solution that could be an alternative to voice controls. While the recent news of Ultraleap’s layoffs is saddening, it may reflect that the company pivoted away from exclusively using its own hardware too late.
Anduril Enters The XR Arena
Oculus founder Palmer Luckey—one of the inaugural 101 members of the XR Hall of Fame announced a couple of months ago—always draws a crowd at AWE. During his panel with Big Screen’s Darshan Shankar, moderated by Stephanie Riggs, Luckey talked about the beginnings of Oculus, then shifted towards talking about his new defense contracting firm, Anduril. (If “Anduril” sounds familiar, it’s the name of Aragorn’s sword in Lord of the Rings.)
The new company is actively developing its own VR headset, driven by military requirements but also available for, in Luckey’s words, “non-military stuff.” During the panel, he specifically called on companies to contact him if they have developed specific structured light-based systems in the right wavelengths. This probably means that Anduril’s product is still very early in its development phase, but we could see Anduril trying to compete with the likes of Varjo and HTC soon.
Campfire Comes To Vision Pro
Campfire started as the rebirth of what was known as Meta AR. It has since been transformed into a collaboration platform powered by a mix of AR and MR headsets. Campfire’s growth since it launched on the Meta Quest 3 last year has been nothing short of gangbusters, with its customer base growing by as much as 50x according to the company’s own metrics. On the vendor side, Campfire has helped numerous companies in different industries with improving development cycles, increasing sales and heading off manufacturing issues.
With the arrival of the Apple Vision Pro headset earlier this year, it seemed inevitable that Campfire would soon launch on the Vision Pro. Now that it did that at AWE, Campfire is one of the few truly cross-platform collaboration tools that spans VisionOS, Horizon OS, iPadOS, Windows and MacOS—and even functions as a browser-based application. It seems that Campfire has moved on from providing its own first-party hardware, which seemed like a means to an end for enabling it on as many headsets as possible and creating a complete collaborative holographic platform.
Varjo Teleports Into Gaussian Splats
At AWE 2024, I had a chance to meet with the team from Varjo and finally try out its latest mixed reality headset, the XR-4, but also try out the company’s new Teleport tool. Varjo Teleport is a great way for people to easily and cheaply produce volumetric environments using an iPhone 12 Pro or newer. The technology that enables these volumetric environments, commonly referred to as photogrammetry, is Gaussian splats, which utilize AI to process images much faster and with greater fidelity than basic photogrammetry. This could be a valuable way for people to share scans of objects and scenes without having to spend too much time or resources creating them. Teleport will work on Varjo’s own PC-based headsets, or on other PC-based headsets from the major brands that support SteamVR.
Distance Technologies Emerges From Stealth
Speaking of Varjo, two of its founders have departed and created a new company that came out of stealth at AWE 2024. Distance Technologies seeks to change the way we think about heads-up displays and 3-D interfaces. Founders Urho Konttori and Jussi Makinen want to create something that delivers a much wider field of view than current technologies—with potentially infinite depth at the same time.
I believe that automotive and aerospace applications will likely be the best candidates for Distance Technologies’ solution whenever it becomes commercially viable. One of the interesting points that both founders brought up is that current heads-up display technologies take up a lot of the volume in the dashboard, so we could potentially see this technology change vehicle design if it ends up being as compact as they say. Companies such as WayRay are already working on delivering these kinds of capabilities in commercial vehicles, so it will be interesting to see how Distance Technologies competes with WayRay’s Deep Reality Display.
NTT DoCoMo’s Qonoq Launches Its XR Glasses
NTT DoCoMo’s Qonoq division has created a joint venture with Sharp to form Qonoq Devices. This division has built what it says are the world’s first wireless XR glasses powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon AR2 Gen 1 chipset. These XR glasses are actually AR glasses with 6DoF tracking, and they weigh only 125g while also providing up to 1,000 nits of brightness for outdoor use. These glasses are so important because they share compute with the user’s smartphone to process higher-fidelity visuals on the device, reduce the weight of the glasses and improve battery life.
I tried these glasses at the Qualcomm booth during AWE and found them to be solid overall, with good brightness and decent image quality. I don’t know whose waveguides Qonoq is using, but I don’t particularly love the slit-style waveguides because they affect overall image quality. Nevertheless, I believe these XR glasses pave the way for more manufacturers to embrace the AR2 Gen 1 platform for high-quality devices tethered wirelessly to smartphones.
XRAI Goes From App To Glasses
XRAI (pronounced X-ray) was an app that I tried in Qualcomm’s booth at MWC 2023. That demo paired XRAI’s real-time translation capabilities with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Spaces using Lenovo ThinkReality A3 glasses. I always thought of this as an app that would live on your smartphone and be displayed on your AR glasses, but now it seems that the team at XRAI has decided not to wait for that future and instead to build its own AR glasses to speed up adoption.
These glasses are extremely limited in resolution, but their only purpose is to show text, which they do really well. The XRAI glasses are powered by a Snapdragon 4100 Wear processor, which is similar to the chip found in Meta’s first-generation Ray-Ban glasses. I would have loved to see them go with an AR1 Gen 1 chipset, but these glasses seem to focus on power conservation above all else. The smartphone app still drives the experience, but now it’s fully wireless and cable-free—and it worked really well even in a congested and noisy environment.
Lucid Reality Labs’ Red Cross Lifeguard Training App
One of the more impactful experiences I had at AWE 2024 was at the Lucid Reality Labs booth, where I tried out the company’s Lifeguard VR training application. The company built this app in partnership with the American Red Cross to deliver a suite of tools to help train hundreds of thousands of lifeguards annually. The idea is to expose lifeguards to scenarios that might not be easy to recreate or might not happen very frequently, but that are still important to be trained for, with drowning scenarios as a prime example.
The American Red Cross wants to train 300,000 users per year using this new VR tool to help narrow the skill gaps among lifeguards and ensure the highest level of safety. If even one life is saved, it will have been worth it. I tried out the drowning simulator and it was extremely realistic, to the point where I felt some of the mental load faced by lifeguards who must always remain aware and watchful for people who might be drowning. While this app didn’t feature eye tracking, that seems like the natural next step in learning how users perform.
Moving XR Forward
Much of what I saw at AWE 2024 highlighted how the industry is moving forward in meaningful ways, especially by continuing to leverage AI to enhance XR experiences. While we haven’t seen XR as the interface for AI yet, I think that the DigiLens ARGO using Google Gemini may get us there sooner rather than later. The industry is clearly converging around certain technologies and design concepts, and I hope that open standards including OpenXR will continue to serve the industry as it travels that positive road. I think that AWE 2024 was a huge success for thriving in a new venue and acknowledging so many of the industry’s veterans in the show’s 15th year.
Thinking about the state of the XR landscape, I believe that some people expected that Apple Vision Pro would have a bigger impact on the XR market by now; but we are still in the early days of Apple’s presence in this market, and the company only recently started shipping the Vision Pro outside of the U.S. and Canada. Meanwhile, I believe that people are still sleeping on companies like XREAL. I believe that the Beam Pro may mark a huge change in the AR ecosystem for consumers, especially with the industry being so enterprise-focused today. My next order of business is to publish my “state of XR” overview, which will be a multi-part series that looks at the entire landscape, how far we’ve come as an industry and where we have yet to go.

title: Council Post: The Evolving Role Of Technology In Market Research
text:
James Whaley is the CEO of OvationMR.
Recent advancements in generative AI and machine learning are changing the ways data analytics and market research are conducted. Practitioners and consumers of market insights can leverage new algorithms to develop deeper insights faster than ever. But these technologies are not immediate problem-solvers. Firms must understand the best marketing applications of generative AI to harness their full potential—responsibly freeing practitioners from repetitive tasks and enabling them to focus on higher level tasks.
How is AI affecting market research?
Traditional analytics has historically been used to perform statistical analysis on large collections of data. While helpful, it is primarily retrospective in nature. These data points—which rely on static models—lack the capability to generate new insights or help predict future changes. In a dynamic economy, focusing on past performance may be a disadvantage.
Generative AI models such as ChatGPT are trained on massive databases of information but those databases are not infinite, so chat models aren’t always responsive to the context you want them to work in. This leads to “hallucinations,” which produce errors. The best way to secure the benefits of AI while eliminating risks is to work with experts who maintain your system. Humans are still best at identifying bias, ethics and privacy issues. For teams that put too much trust in tools built on external data, their successes are at constant risk of mistakes due to lack of human oversight.
Instead of trusting their sensitive data to public databases, many teams opt to build their own AI for research purposes. An internal chatbot can be specifically trained on your data, eliminating bias and most hallucinations from the system. Plus, training on internal data enables you to ask questions like, “What was the competition like between these two major soda brands between 1990 and 1995, and which marketing campaigns affected the results the most?” These types of questions provide powerful insights that could not be derived from a public AI.
Most businesses know they want to invest in AI for some of their data analysis. A more productive question is whether they want to build their own product or partner with an AI company. To understand the best decision for your firm, consider how these traditional challenges in market research will change with new technology developments.
Data Cleaning
One of the most important tasks in market research is data cleaning. As analysts, we must ensure our data is based on valid responses. This has always been the case with data analytics—you get out what you put in—but is even more critical in the age of artificial intelligence.
If your firm creates and interprets data from a large number of surveys, you already know this is an arduous task when performed manually. As a result, many firms are tempted to outsource all of their data cleaning to an AI solution. While this is a great application of AI, excessive trust in algorithms risks missing mistakes in data which can result in exponentially worse errors.
Many firms prefer working with companies that emphasize high quality data collection to mitigate this risk. They seek partnerships with companies that specialize in using AI to identify large blocks of text for efficient human screening. This saves a lot of time in the process of data cleaning while upholding the importance of human insights. An ideal partner will have a deep understanding of how generative models should (and should not) be used for data cleaning.
If you are approaching the development of your own AI product, this should be considered with your internal team. Do you have the capacity to maintain a significant level of focus on data cleaning? If not, a partnership with the right firm may be in your best interest.
Survey Depth
Survey insights have traditionally been limited by quantitative analysis. For example, in a standard survey for a banking service, you may ask participants to rate the service on a scale of one through 10. But what do these data points tell you about your business? More often than not, firms must arrange follow-up qualitative interviews. This deeper dive with respondents yields meaningful insights at a steep cost, both of time and money.
Instead, with a properly trained AI model, you can design your survey to include interactive elements that prompt qualitative responses. For example, if a respondent gives a score of 90%, which we know falls at the high end of the Net Promoter Score, a properly trained chat feature can ask a follow-up question and probe further if needed, diving deeper into what an individual customer likes and dislikes about your service. You may find that loyal customers have problems with your company, allowing you to revisit your strategy in a more proactive manner. To set this up properly, you need to either partner with a company who has expertise in training AI models or have the capability to hire experts for your team as required.
Data cleaning is even more important when using surveys with qualitative elements. This further emphasizes the importance of your dedication to maintaining data quality. If you plan to include qualitative chat elements in your otherwise quantitative survey, it is important to work with experts that understand how to use machine learning with very large data sets. This skillset extends far beyond expertise in chatbot functionality.
If you want AI to perform both data cleaning and qualitative functionality in your customer surveys, you may want to partner with a market research company with expertise in artificial intelligence. The specialized knowledge required is often too much for an internal team to assume. Plus, working with a trusted provider helps mitigate risks—and liabilities—of working with these new and powerful technologies.

title: 3 Things You May Not Realize Are Impacting Your Customer Satisfaction Score
text:
The most successful brands understand that high quality customer service provides a distinct competitive advantage. It’s no longer good enough to provide an acceptable customer experience– today’s customer journey must be exceptional at every step. With businesses losing a total of $75 billion due to poor customer service, the stakes are too high not to make customer service a long-term strategic imperative.
Customer satisfaction should be every brand’s North Star, guiding companies as they work to exceed customer expectations. Most brands use CSAT (Customer Satisfaction Score) to measure how satisfied customers are with their product or services, typically accomplished through surveys or questionnaires. CSAT can provide brands with invaluable customer feedback while serving as a solid indicator of customer loyalty and retention. But a low CSAT score can negatively impact the relationship you have with your customers. In fact, our company’s research shows that 85% of consumers would avoid a brand due to bad customer service.
To keep your customers loyal and coming back for more, it’s helpful to understand what may be contributing to a lower-than-desired CSAT score. Here are three surprising factors that may be getting in the way of customer satisfaction:
Waiting for an SOS signal.
The biggest piece of advice I can offer to modern brands is to unravel and address the customer story before it even unfolds. Too many brands wait for a customer to reach out with a problem. The problem is that today’s customers aren’t looking for reactive customer service. They want you to proactively anticipate and predict your needs from the get-go, starting the customer service journey with a “hello” rather than a “help.”
Instead of activating customer service solutions when a customer may already be feeling frustrated, start engaging with customers the moment they first interact with your brand. Here’s where the right CRM can make all the difference. Look for a CRM that captures critical data upfront, enabling anticipatory services that address needs before they become problems. Look for technology that captures key data at order placement, not ticket time, so that you’re catching any problems from the starting line, not halfway through the race. CRMs equipped to prepare for the future based on current observations, data, or trends are the key to delivering exceptional service and staying ahead of your competitors.
Improper use of AI.
Most brands would agree that artificial intelligence has revolutionized how businesses handle customer interactions, from automated responses to predictive analytics. When implemented correctly, AI can streamline processes, provide personalized customer experiences, and improve overall satisfaction. However, improper use or implementation can have adverse effects, leading to frustration and dissatisfaction among customers.
Imagine a scenario where a customer contacts your company with a complex issue. Your AI functionality, designed to handle routine inquiries efficiently, struggles to comprehend the nuanced problem and provides generic responses that do not address the customer's concerns. This situation escalates as the customer grows increasingly frustrated with the inability to reach a human representative who can provide a tailored solution.
To avoid these repercussions, make sure that your AI sets your customer service team up for success, empowering them to deliver a seamless and efficient customer experience. Look for a CRM system that uses advanced data analytics and AI-driven algorithms that help you gather, analyze and interpret customer data to create the highest levels of personalization. Make sure that whatever platform you choose uses AI-fueled process guidance and decisioning to guide users through the best actions and conversations.
Chatbots activated too late.
Research shows that approximately 1.5 billion people are using chatbots, and that number is only going to increase. By 2027, chatbots are expected to become the primary customer service channel for one-quarter of businesses. According to Accenture, 57% of businesses agree that conversational bots can deliver large return on investment for minimal effort. If you’re utilizing AI chatbots in your customer service practices, it’s essential to think about when your AI chatbot comes into play. After all, chatbots are designed for efficiency and availability around the clock. However, deploying them too late in the customer journey can lead to the opposite effect, increasing instead of decreasing customer frustration and dissatisfaction.
Set up your system so that AI chatbots offer guidance and help before a customer has a chance to initiate outreach to your customer service team. In other words, your chatbot should say "What can I help you find today?" the first moment a customer comes to your website. And with Gartner predicting chatbots will become the primary customer service channel by 2027, the sooner you bring chatbots into your customer service strategy the better.
Boosting your CSAT starts the very first moment a customer interacts with your brand and continues through every step of the journey. Whether it’s leveraging customer data and insights to prove that you know what customers want and need, harnessing AI to smooth out any bumps along the way, or making the most of chatbots to showcase your 24/7 availability, you have the power to make sure that your CSAT is truly reflective of the superior experience your brand is delivering.

title: Billions Of People Need To Learn AI Literacy
text:
What is AI literacy? And why is it important?
Let’s start with the second one first. The reason that AI literacy is critical is that AI is the new immersive technology.
First we had actual literacy, “literacy 1.0,” that distinguished the power elites of the first millennium (and first half of the second millennium) from the common folk. Literacy was power! Then, very recently in the grand scheme of things, we had computer literacy: the “haves” knowing how to, say, operate Microsoft Excel.
Now, suddenly, we have the need for AI literacy, the same kinds of gaps in power that arise with any literacy movement, where first movers will gain exceptional power, and everyone else will be, to an extent, left behind.
So then, what is AI literacy? It’s a good question, because, unlike “literacy 1.0,” the answer is pretty complex.
The test of the initial type of literacy was simply: Can you read? Or, how well can you read? There are about 50 symbols, give or take, on a page. It’s measurable – and we do measure it, for every child, everywhere in the country.
AI literacy, on the other hand…
I came across this definition by Matt Crabtree at Data Camp. He describes AI literacy in detail, but includes this:
“It's about viewing these technologies critically, understanding their context, and questioning their design and implementation. It's also about being able to discern the benefits and challenges of AI while making informed decisions about its use.”
So at its core, it’s more about manipulating reality with technologies than it is about memorizing word spelling or sounding out phonetics. It’s just a different animal.
Here’s more from a recent presentation by Chis McKay at IIA, who started out with a call to action and a cautionary example of siloed knowledge.
“The most important thing that we can do as individuals, as businesses, and as a society, in my opinion, is to invest in AI literacy,” McKay said. “You see, history is full of examples where ignorance has led to downfall. In fact, if you think of the last few years that we've been through, during the COVID pandemic, we lived and saw firsthand what the lack of health literacy did for a lot of our communities. We can't make that mistake again.”
Later, he narrated a key moment in AI adoption, just recently, in a way that I think tells us a lot about what has been going on:
“I looked to my social feed, and it was crazy, right? You had people that were hyping AI promising a new techno-utopia, you had people that were saying it was going to lead to the end of the world, and others that were saying it was just a fad, right? There were loud voices on both ends, you know, P Doom 99.99%. But I also looked at our legislatures and our leaders, and I saw people that were out of their depths - I looked at our educators and our teachers, and I really wondered if they were at risk of getting left behind. I looked at other business owners, and I saw that a lot of them had a lot of the same questions that I did.”
So, ultimately, McKay created a platform, imaginator.com, to delve into AI.
“I come to you with a unique perspective,” he said. “Not only am I covering the AI space, so I'm fully aware of where the technology is, where it's going. But I'm also working with companies that are applying it in their businesses and in consumer products. And what is AI literacy? AI literacy is being able to understand to evaluate and to make informed decisions about AI.”
He made this critical distinction:
“I'm not saying you need to go out and get a PhD in this stuff. You don't need to know the latest rack optimization techniques. But you do need to know how to use it.”
AI literacy, he suggested, will come with a range of pretty important social benefits, especially if it is broadly applied.
“It will allow us to ask better questions,” he said. “Ai literacy means that we can have deeper conversations, but also include more voices in the conversation. AI is something that needs to be decided and discussed by as many voices as possible. And ensuring that we can bring more people to the table will be critical. But most importantly, it will allow us to develop effective oversight, better regulation and governance, and ultimately, hopefully, leverage this technology to improve our everyday lives.”
Relating all of this to business, he talked about strategy, and recommended a book: Life 3.0 by Max Tegmark. I have written about Max’s work, too, so this was a good reference, in my opinion.
Here are a couple of other assertions he made: “application is going to be key,” and “continuous learning is non-negotiable.” I like those.
So think about it, as you move further into the AI space. How do we increase this new kind of literacy? What programs and interventions are going to work?

title: SAP BrandVoice: Digitalization Is The First Step In Powering Clean Mobility
text:
The powertrain is the mechanism that transmits the drive from the engine of a vehicle to its axle. Our entire concept of mobility depends on the powertrain, because no car, truck, or motorbike can move without it.
Until now, the powertrain was mostly used with combustion engines, which have been used to transport people and goods around the world since the 1860s. The only problem is that combustion engines burn fossil fuels that release greenhouse gases and other pollutants, contributing to global warming and air pollution.
“At Vitesco Technologies, we don’t just talk about transformation, we are the transformation,” said Thomas Buck, CIO, Vitesco Technologies, a company that is leading the development of innovative, efficient electrification technologies for all types of vehicles.
bbSpeaking at the recent SAP Sapphire event in Barcelona, Buck explained how the company is powering the future with clean mobility.
“Our goal is to move from today’s 90% combustion model to a 90% electrified model by 2050,” he said. “Our powertrain technologies cover the systems of today and tomorrow, providing hybrid solutions along the way.”
With 35,500 employees in 50 locations around the globe, the mission of Vitesco Technologies is to reduce the environmental impacts of the automotive industry worldwide and promote emission-free mobility in the long term. This massive task cannot be achieved without continuously evolving technology – be it the engineering kind or the computational kind.
The company is a spinoff from Continental, a German automotive company with a long legacy of innovation in tires, brake systems, vehicle electronics, and much more. Because the powertrain is such a critical element in an automobile, the board made a strategic decision to make it an independent entity, creating Vitesco Technologies, which takes its name from the word “vital.”
“We need to balance electrification with maintaining a profitable core business,” said Buck, referring to the fact that Vitesco Technologies’ profitable combustion business is what will finance the new electrification model. “There are countless challenges and opportunities as we transition to sustainable mobility. Digitalization is a key part of our strategy, and it’s the foundation for leveraging generative AI to enhance business operations.”
The benefits are already apparent. Buck explained that Vitesco inherited a very fragmented ERP landscape, and his team was tasked with harmonizing and migrating to SAP S/4HANA with the RISE with SAP offering. Now, Vitesco Technologies has a platform that will help improve business processes, provide stability and security, and help reduce costs. Being in the cloud will accelerate its other transformation activities.
“We share SAP’s belief that the cloud is the basis for innovation, and we’re using SAP Business Technology Platform to enable low-code and no-code scenarios for employees,” said Buck. “The SAP Datasphere solution will play a significant role in our next steps. We’re really eager to see the first use case with the Joule copilot, SAP’s new generative AI assistant.”
From his perspective as the CIO, Buck sees two critical success factors to be a digital winner. Number one is the ability to adopt new technology quickly, because time to market is crucial. He and his team dedicate a lot of time and thought to speeding up processes.
Buck sees digitalization as a competitive advantage. It’s not enough to digitalize; speed is the differentiator. Cloud computing facilitates on-demand access to scalable computing resources and faster development, testing, and deployment of digital solutions. It starts with basics such as having the right architecture in place.
The second important point is that digitalization must be a company-wide effort. “Every organization in the company must participate to eliminate bottlenecks. Most importantly, you have to make sure everyone has access to relevant data,” he said.
When it comes to generative AI, Buck pointed out that you don’t always need the most complex model for every task. Most people are talking about large language models, but working with a small language model has definite advantages.
A model like ChatGPT handles all the data of the world, so it might work well for generic questions but not in a business context, where you need very specific data.
For example, if you are working in the area of requirements engineering or product development, you may already have a set of specifications, and if you want to add new ones, you’ll just want the model to compare specific sets. At the same time, it’s important to use your own data. Anyone can use a generative AI model, but the quality of your data is what creates the competitive advantage.
“Right now, we’re still learning and experimenting,” said Buck. “The really exciting part will be when we start putting the pieces together and can start visualizing our entire factory in the metaverse, for example, instead of just designing a product in 3D.”
The other exciting aspect of digitalization is that it enables organizations to track a product's carbon footprint across the supply chain, providing transparency into opportunities for decarbonization, a key element in Vitesco Technologies’ sustainability agenda.
“This is how we are powering the future with clean mobility,” said Buck.

title: Britain's new government aims to regulate most powerful AI models - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet
- 2 min read
Britain's new government aims to regulate most powerful AI models
The government said it would seek to establish the appropriate legislation to place requirements on those working to develop "the most powerful artificial intelligence models."
Britain's new Labour government has said it will explore how to effectively regulate artificial intelligence models, but stopped short of proposing any specific laws.
King Charles set out newly elected Prime Minister Keir Starmer's legislative agenda in a speech on Wednesday to open the new session of parliament. It included more than 35 new bills covering everything from housing to cyber security measures.
The government said it would seek to establish the appropriate legislation to place requirements on those working to develop "the most powerful artificial intelligence models."
The country's last prime minister Rishi Sunak had sought to position Britain as a world leader in AI safety, bringing world leaders and company executives together last November for a summit at Bletchley Park to discuss the issue.
He also oversaw the launch of the world's first AI Safety Institute, which has focused on the capabilities of "frontier" AI models, such as those behind OpenAI's highly successful ChatGPT chatbot.
"AI labs will be collectively breathing a sigh of relief at the government's decision not to rush ahead with frontier model regulation," said Nathan Benaich, founding partner of AI-focused investment group Air Street Capital.
Under Sunak, the government avoided introducing targeted AI regulation, opting instead to split responsibility for scrutinizing the technology between various regulators.
Starmer has promised to introduce new laws on AI, but his government is taking a careful approach to rolling them out.
"The UK's cautious, sector-based approach to AI regulation remains a crucial competitive advantage versus the EU, and any moves to change this regime should only be taken with the utmost caution," Benaich said.
But some AI experts say the rapid rollout of AI tools over the past 18 months only makes the need for new legislation more urgent.
Gaia Marcus, director of the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the government should bring forward a bill as soon as possible.
"These systems are already being integrated into our daily lives, our public services and our economy, bringing benefits and opportunity, but also posing a range of risks to people and society," she said.

title: Council Post: The Executive Playbook For Generative AI: Turning Potential Into Business Value
text:
Ram Menon is the Founder and CEO of Avaamo, a generative AI leader for the enterprise.
2024 is the year generative AI moves beyond stargazing. Heady rhetoric—like how AI is an invention “almost like” the printing press—obscures what’s actually important for business leaders today.
The focus should instead be on how businesses can implement AI in ways that automate workflows end-to-end and drive immediate value, all while mitigating risks and ensuring compliance. Unlike the mixed messages in the market today, the reality is that this is achievable today.
Step 1: Choose the business output you want to transform first.
Choose a business output or workflow you want to transform first. This depends on your priorities but can be anything from fulfilling IT requests and resolving tickets more efficiently to managing employee car service reservations and filing corresponding expense reports.
VC and industry vet Chamath Palihapitiya frequently makes the astute comparison that data is the “new oil” and AI tools and software are the refineries. They’re all approaching the opportunity in different ways, refining data into an infinitely valuable resource.
The applications are the output. Just like we use oil for everything from powering jets to producing plastics, those end-user “outputs” and the tangible workflows you transform via automation are what ultimately matter most for a business, not the nitty-gritty specifications of an underlying LLM.
Step 2: Move quickly, but be methodical.
Companies looking to score early wins with GenAI should move quickly; however, not at the expense of being methodical. Those hoping that GenAI offers a shortcut past the tough—and necessary—detailed analysis of business outputs will likely yield disappointing results. Launching a pilot AI workflow is (relatively) easy, but getting those pilots to scale and create meaningful value is hard. This is because they require a broad set of changes in the way work actually gets done.
The broad excitement around generative AI and its relative ease of use has led to a burst of experimentation across organizations. Most of these initiatives, however, won’t generate a true competitive advantage. For example, a customer informed me they previously bought multiple licenses of a major developer platform’s copilot tool, but since they didn’t have a clear sense of how to work with the technology, progress was slow.
Other unfocused efforts typically revolve around experimenting with multiple vendor tools at the same time or using multiple LLM interfaces without a cohesive goal in place. Avoid these pitfalls by building your approach parameters, objectives and processes in advance.
Step 3: Create and deploy a unified implementation plan.
For enterprise leaders under pressure to understand, monitor and adopt AI for their organization, focus on driving near-term value by aligning GenAI efforts to your internal end users’ current roles.
Focus on improving and automating workflows, such as your procurement manager sourcing multiple products across departments, the salesperson in Chicago who needs enablement for selling a brand-new product or a customer service manager resolving dozens of queries before lunch.
Consider a real-world example.
It’s important to ground all rhetoric about AI in reality. Here’s an example of a real GenAI implementation that illustrates the three steps outlined above.
A global systems integrator adopted generative AI with a razor-sharp focus on business outputs. They first chose to implement it in their human resources department. The reason was that it had an internal domain, a secure authentication infrastructure in place and a reduced transaction risk.
They set about engaging their business users along with a GenAI software partner to analyze traditional workflows and business outputs deeply like automating time sheets, travel policies and benefits management. All these seemingly “mundane” business outputs were analyzed for efficiency and then plotted on how generative AI could improve and transform the experience for employees.
The results? Just 15 months later, the company had 40-plus use cases automated for daily tasks and auto-resolved 6.5 million queries in a safe, compliant manner. This translates to hundreds of thousands of dollars in workforce labor savings and counting.
Generative AI has the opportunity to radically transform the enterprise. By the end of this year, over 77% of companies will either be using or exploring AI in their organization. But at the end of the day, it matters how their implementation ultimately impacts business output. Business leaders care that it makes their lives easier and drives results—and, more likely than not, they couldn’t care less about which LLM is behind it.
